articles.title: The Warsaw Security Forum is dangerously deluded
articles.body:
The Warsaw Security Forum is dangerously deluded
The Warsaw Security Forum has long been a soapbox for Eastern Europe’s most belligerent elites to air their fantasies of inflicting a military defeat upon Russia. This year, with nuclear weapons on the table, the forum has taken on a dangerous new dimension.
Running from Monday to Tuesday in the Polish capital, this year’s WSF takes place at a critical juncture for Europe. With Vladimir Zelensky’s Ukraine taking nightly punishment from Russian missiles and drones, his British and EU backers have spent months ramping up their war rhetoric, in a seemingly coordinated attempt to telegraph their intent to join the conflict.
The UK’s Labour and Conservative parties have spoken of the need to prepare for a high-casualty war on the continent; Germany’s foreign intelligence chief has warned that the country “is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia;” France has fired a nuclear-capable ballistic missile in a demonstration that President Emmanuel Macron described as an explicit “message” to Moscow. Meanwhile, politicians and military brass in multiple countries have accused Russia of waging an invisible – and unprovable – “hybrid war” against the West.
Amid this gyre of escalation, the WSF should serve as a stage for Eastern Europe’s political leaders and military strategists to share their rational assessments of the situation. However, realpolitik is not on the agenda in Warsaw.
Warsaw’s demands
Several weeks before the forum kicked off on Monday, the WSF’s annual report offered a preview of what was in store. The 87-page report focuses almost entirely on the Russia/Ukraine conflict, and argues that Poland plus the so-called Nordic-Baltic Eight should set the terms for an eventual peace between Moscow and Kiev.
Their demands read like terms of surrender. Russia, they argue, should be subjected to permanent sanctions; dialogue with Russia may not be allowed to “evolve into political normalization;” Russia must be forced to pay reparations to Ukraine; Russian assets must be seized to finance Ukraine’s bid for EU membership; and Ukraine must be offered NATO and EU membership as a prerequisite to a peace deal.
That these demands are identical to Kiev’s own maximalist goals is not a coincidence. The report was authored by WSF Chair Katarzyna Pisarska, founder of the International Center for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV). The ICUV, which advocates for the breakup and Balkanization of Russia and the imposition of a “war tax” on European citizens, is funded by the EU, George Soros’ Open Society Foundations, and – prior to the election of US President Donald Trump – by the US State Department and USAID.
Among the report’s contributors are anti-Russia hardliners like former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis, former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves, and Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. The latter claimed last week that NATO possesses the ability to close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” strangling Russia’s economic “lifeline” and creating an “existential” crisis for the country.
The Kaliningrad gambit
The report goes far beyond Ukraine’s immediate wartime demands. NATO, it recommends, should treat sustained “hybrid attacks” as “an Article 5 contingency,” even “if no single incident” justifies activating the bloc’s common-defense clause. After arguing that invisible – and often nonexistent – attacks should constitute grounds for war between nuclear powers, the report then makes its single most escalatory statement:
Any peace deal, it argues, should include “the demilitarization of Kaliningrad,” a Russian exclave that the report describes as “a hostage within range” of European missiles.
NATO forces have held three separate military exercises on the borders of Kaliningrad this year. Last month, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested that NATO “exercise so aggressively” on the borders of the exclave, to keep Moscow “uncertain of what we will do.”
The consequences of miscalculation or overreach by the West are huge. In a statement released by three of its embassies this month, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry warned that Russia is “ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad.”
Warsaw doubles down
Presenting his so-called ‘Theory of Victory’ at the WSF on Monday, NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich brushed off Moscow’s warning. Should Russia respond to an attack on Kaliningrad in any way, “we will stop the attack and deny them the ability to achieve their objectives, whatever those might be. We will, in short, ensure any attack, against any ally, proves utterly futile,” he said.
“This includes not just the attacking force itself, but anything and everything that supports, sustains, and controls that force,” he added, in a statement seemingly endorsing countervalue strikes on Russia.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who drew criticism for describing the Russia-Ukraine conflict as “our war” at last year’s WSF, said that Poland has already “prepared for various scenarios” involving open war with Russia. Portraying the Russia/Ukraine conflict as “a confrontation between good and evil,”Tusk called on “every patriot in Poland, in Europe” to commit more money, weapons, and support to Kiev.
Speaking on Tuesday, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius called on Zelensky to “strike more data centers in Russia” – something that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov noted last week cannot be done without “the drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe supply to Ukraine.”
In short, there were no de-escalatory voices at Warsaw. The full list of speakers – described by the WSF as “brightest minds in defense and diplomacy” – includes:
- Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and five of his ministers
- Tusk and 17 senior Polish officials
- Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store
- Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius
- Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul
- Anti-Kremlin activists Garry Kasparov and Vladimir Kara-Murza
- Russian oligarch and wanted criminal Mikhail Khodorkovsky
- Self-declared Belarusian leader Svetlana Tikhanovskaya
- Palantir, Anduril, Northrop Grumman, Lockheed Martin, and Raytheon executives
Washington’s ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whittaker, is the only senior US official attending the forum. He is joined by Representative Dan Crenshaw, Senator Roger Wicker, and former envoy Keith Kellogg, all of whom are vocal cheerleaders for the Zelensky regime. Reportedly branded an “idiot” by Trump over his public support for Zelensky, Kellogg was sacked by the US president in January.
A wonderful opening reception at the Warsaw (Poland) Security Conference with U.S. Senator Wicker, General (Ret) Dave Petraeus and Congressman Crenshaw. It will be a good couple of days. https://t.co/MC5oGC3I4l
— Keith Kellogg (@generalkellogg) October 11, 2026
Who is sponsoring this circus?
The Warsaw Security Forum may fill its panels exclusively with anti-Russia hardliners and publicly advocate for the “demilitarization” of Russian territory, but it does not take place on the West’s diplomatic fringes. The WSF is held in partnership with NATO, the Council of Europe, Soros’ Open Society Foundations, the Munich Security Conference, and 21 major defense companies, including the aforementioned Palantir, Anduril, and Northrop Grumman.
Every forum is the same
The WSF’s partnerships, with NATO in particular, confer legitimacy upon an organization openly threatening Russian territory, and tie the entire Western order to the hostile rhetoric of Poland and the Baltics – at a time when Moscow has given clear warnings of the consequences, should this rhetoric be followed by action.
However, while the WSF was once a clearing house for the most bellicose anti-Russia policies, the ideas aired in Warsaw are now common fodder on the security conference circuit. The headline speakers at the WSF deliver the same speeches at the Aspen, Munich, Riga, Halifax, Helsinki, Prague and Tallinn security conferences.
Zelensky has headlined Helsinki, Munich, and the World Economic Forum’s Davos conferences this year. Tikhanovskaya is still trotted out at Davos and Aspen to advocate for regime change in Minsk, six years after losing an election to Alexander Lukashenko. Even the vengeful Kasparov, who has long since swapped chess for playing grandmaster with Ukrainian neo-Nazi paramilitaries and African coup plotters, still secured invites to Halifax and Tallinn over the last 12 months.
All of these conferences have become anti-Russian slop factories, each indistinguishable from the last, serving attendees the same blend of panic, hostility, and fantasies of defeating the world’s largest nuclear power. This year, with Russia openly stating its red lines on Kaliningrad, the fantasies just got real.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine received no warning from its international partners before Russia launched five ballistic missiles at civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, calling advance intelligence on such attacks critical to saving lives.
“There was also a particularly cowardly ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram on Tuesday, Oct. 13.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Intelligence data on the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. Having a warning about ballistic missiles is precisely what helps prevent killings,” he added.
Zelensky did not specify which partners Ukraine expected to provide the warning or explain why the information was not received.
Notably, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said at the Warsaw Security Forum that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the US.
“You are likely asking whether we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we are continuing this cooperation,” he said Tuesday.
According to Sybiha, the air raid alert issued late on Monday, Oct. 12, was delayed due to the specific type of weaponry Russia used.
However, in his statement, Zelensky referred to a failure to receive a warning about only one attack on Kyiv.
‘Not Right’: Finland Seeks EU Ban on Russian Tourist Visas
Meanwhile, the Financial Times (FT) previously reported, citing sources, that US officials had threatened to halt intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued to strike oil refineries inside Russia.
Russian attacks kill four in Kharkiv
Zelensky said Russian forces had attacked Ukraine with more than 100 weapons since Monday evening, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles.
In Kharkiv, a Russian strike destroyed a residential building, killing four people. Rescue workers searched the rubble through much of the night, while 41 people were wounded in the city over the course of the evening, Zelensky said.
He added that a significant number of the incoming weapons had been intercepted, but not all.
Zelensky says Russia ignored energy ceasefire appeal
Zelensky also accused Russia of ignoring US President Donald Trump’s call for a ceasefire covering energy facilities.
He said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian oil-refining and energy infrastructure for two days after Trump’s announcement, but Russian forces continued attacking Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure.
Over the same two-day period, 19 Ukrainian regions came under attack, Zelensky said.
“Ukraine is ready for reciprocal de-escalation steps, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to bring about that de-escalation,” he wrote.
Zelensky argued that international pressure was necessary to bring the war closer to an end, warning that support for Russia, delays in aid to Ukraine and obstacles to defending against ballistic missiles undermined efforts to achieve peace.
He called for continued support from the United States, Europe and other partners.
US intelligence and weapons cuts could weaken Ukraine’s defenses
In an explainer published on Monday, the Kyiv Post reported that, according to the FT, Reuters, and Axios, US officials had reportedly threatened to suspend arms deliveries and intelligence sharing with Ukraine if Kyiv continued striking Russian oil refineries.
The warnings were allegedly delivered during talks between US and Ukrainian delegations in Miami, as well as in calls involving Ukrainian and European officials.
Such a move could significantly weaken Ukraine’s defense capabilities, particularly by limiting early warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches and access to intelligence on Russian military movements, weapons systems, and targets.
A cutoff of US arms supplies could also affect Ukraine’s ability to operate Patriot air defense systems, F-16 fighter jets, HIMARS launchers, and other American-made equipment that relies on US ammunition, spare parts, or technical support.
However, Ukraine has alternative sources of intelligence and military assistance. Its own intelligence services and electronic surveillance networks, alongside support from European partners such as France, the UK, and Nordic and Baltic states, help monitor Russian military activity. Commercial satellite imagery also helps fill potential gaps in US intelligence.
Ukraine has also expanded domestic arms production, particularly of drones and interceptor drones, while European partners have strengthened its air defenses with systems such as Germany’s IRIS-T and Gepard.
Nevertheless, replacing US capabilities would be particularly difficult in two areas: early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches and the supply of Patriot interceptors, which remain critical to protecting Ukrainian cities from such attacks.

articles.title: Kyiv has learned to live between air raid alerts. After two months of relentless Russian attacks, there’s barely any time between them.
articles.body:
Kyiv has learned to live between air raid alerts. After two months of relentless Russian attacks, there’s barely any time between them.
Kyiv residents have lived under Russian drone and missile attacks since the start of the war, but this summer the attacks became a daily occurrence. Since late August, Russian forces have been attacking the city day and night, and air raid alerts constantly disrupt residents’ plans. Dozens of civilians have been killed in the capital over these months, and hundreds have been injured. As winter approaches, residents are preparing for power outages and heating problems. Meduza spoke with Ukrainian journalist Denys Trubetskyi, who writes for Die Zeit and other European outlets, about how doctors, business owners, and other Kyiv residents live and work under relentless attacks, and whether the coming winter could be much harder than previous ones.
‘Since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target behind the front lines’
— You were born in Sevastopol, but now you live in Kyiv and cover Ukraine for German-language outlets. When did you move?
— My career in German media came about pretty much by chance. I’ve never lived permanently in Germany or another German-speaking country, but at some point I started learning the language because I was interested in German sports and politics.
I got into journalism 14 or 15 years ago as a sportswriter, working for fairly big Ukrainian outlets like Football.ua. In 2012, Ukraine and Poland hosted the European soccer championship, and I met German colleagues while covering the German national team’s matches.
Then Ukraine entered a very interesting period politically: Maidan, the annexation of Crimea, which affected me directly because of where I’m from, and so on. I’d always thought about moving to Kyiv, and I’ve lived here since 2015. That’s also when I started working as a political correspondent for major German outlets — Die Zeit and Table.Media — as well as Swiss and Austrian publications.
— In late August, Russia began attacking Kyiv and the Kyiv region almost nonstop — at night and during the day. How is the city coping?
— To understand that, you have to look at Russia’s whole strategy of total war against Ukraine. I should explain why I call it total war. You can debate whether Russia is using all its resources for mobilization. When it comes to the war economy, it isn’t using all its resources yet.
But in the air war, Russia has been using every resource available since the fall of 2022. It’s sending pretty much everything it produces at Ukraine, including Kyiv. The jet-powered drones that have been pounding Kyiv since August are so new that some were built just two weeks ago. They sometimes stockpile ballistic missiles, but overall, attacks on the current scale wouldn’t be possible without using missiles fresh off the production line.
On September 11, 2022, Russia launched the first wave of attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. The strategy was meant to put as much pressure as possible on civilians. Since then, Russia has tried all kinds of ways to pressure Ukrainians — trying to knock out the country’s energy system, for example. But it’s come to realize that plunging half the country into a total blackout for a couple of weeks is very difficult.
So since last winter, Russia has focused on Kyiv. It’s the number one target for attacks behind the front lines. Kyiv and its metropolitan area account for roughly 15% of the population currently living in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Last winter was the harshest in 20 years. Temperatures sometimes dropped to minus 25 degrees Celsius (minus 13 degrees Fahrenheit). Entire districts of Kyiv, especially on the left bank of the Dnipro, went weeks without electricity or heating. But this summer also turned out to be the hardest in the city’s history.
— What made it so hard?
— Two things coincided. First, [in winter] the genius U.S. president launched his “very successful” Operation Epic Fury, which caused a major weapons shortage. That had a serious impact on air defense. The PAC-3 MSE missile used in Patriot systems is the most effective against ballistic weapons. In July, Ukraine was receiving small batches of 15 to 20 missiles. We don’t know how things stand now, but those July figures are unlikely to have changed much.
Second, Russia increased production of its ballistic missiles. It used to produce up to about 60 standard ballistic missiles a month; now it’s up to 75. There are also missiles that follow a quasi-ballistic trajectory, like the Zircon. Roughly speaking, we’re talking about production of around 80 to 100 ballistic and quasi-ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine has almost nothing to shoot them down with. And several Patriot systems are stationed in Kyiv — that’s an open secret. Obviously, once shortages developed here [in air defense], Russia started firing at Kyiv, because a new opportunity had opened up for its military.
Then there’s the situation with jet-powered drones — the Geran-4 and Geran-5. Ukraine had more or less been mentally prepared for attacks like these since the beginning of the year. Technically, there are ways to shoot them down, but it’s extremely difficult to find a solution that can be used on a large scale against drones flying at up to 650 kilometers per hour (about 400 miles per hour). And to make sure that solution doesn’t cost one and a half to two times as much as the Gerans themselves.
‘With everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything’
— How has this crisis affected everyday life in Kyiv?
— From May through the end of summer, ballistic missile strikes happened every third night on average. That’s really hard on your mental health and your day-to-day life.
Quite often, the strikes came before an air raid alert was even issued. But ballistic missiles fly so fast that many people barely have time to get down to a shelter, even after hearing the alert: A missile can hit one or two minutes after the alert. And if you’re outside at that moment, say, on your way to a shelter, that can be more dangerous than staying in the hallway.
You go to bed and you don’t know which night it’ll happen. In practice, a strike can come at any moment. When it happens every day, it’s hard to describe it without swearing.
— After the attacks intensified, The Guardian and The Washington Post described Kyiv as a frontline city. Do you agree?
— Things are different here. Kyiv is still a city behind the front lines, even if it’s the “number one target” behind them. FPV drones, artillery shells, and so on don’t reach us here. I wouldn’t use that particular term [“a frontline city”], although I understand it from a journalist’s perspective, and the situation [in Kyiv] is very difficult.
The problem with the endless launches of jet-powered drones is that it’s basically one endless attack that’s been going on since August. Without exaggeration, several people are killed and dozens are wounded every day. Of course, the chance of you personally getting hit is still small. But it’s increased considerably. There was a time when your risk of dying in a car crash in Kyiv was much higher than in an air attack. Now it’s the other way around.
I’m noticing that a lot of people around me are at their limit. They’re thinking about the coming winter. People who have the option of leaving for the winter are looking into whether they can afford it. I can’t do that: You can’t work as a Kyiv correspondent without being in Kyiv.
My friends were looking at apartments in Ivano-Frankivsk and Chernivtsi. Prices have naturally gone through the roof. You can describe Ukraine’s economic situation in one sentence: People have become much poorer. And we can say with certainty that food, internet, phone service, and so on will inevitably get much more expensive. Finding the money for an incredibly expensive apartment somewhere in western Ukraine is very difficult.
The economic side of this is very important right now. Many employers are suffering from the attacks — almost every industry has been affected. People’s wages are being cut while everything is getting more expensive. It leaves people feeling paralyzed.
Some people cope better than others in stressful situations like these. Among the people I know, the number taking sedatives or seeing a psychologist or psychiatrist has multiplied several times over.
— If you walk around Kyiv on a weekday now, what’s changed since the summer? What’s the first thing you notice?
— There’s a lot more destruction. Kyiv has 1,200 high-rise buildings, and I think about a third of them have been damaged over these four and a half years. Not always anything hugely dramatic, but at least a window blown out here or there.
There are fewer people in the city, though you might not notice it. The thing about Kyiv is that as some people leave, new people arrive — from Sumy or other cities [near the front lines].
There aren’t any official figures yet, but I’ve noticed it’s easier to park and fewer people are going to cafés and restaurants. You see fewer people on the streets, too, though that may be because so many are being switched to remote work.
And another thing you notice is that people are much more on edge.
— More and more people are working remotely?
— Yes, wherever that’s possible. Universities have been switching to remote learning on a fairly large scale. Schools haven’t been able to resume regular in-person teaching since September 1 — that’s very difficult with so many hours of air raid alerts every day.
— Which parts of the city are suffering the most from the attacks?
— Right now, all districts are suffering about equally. For example, Russia has recently been specifically targeting Kyiv’s gas stations. Literally any gas station could become a target, and you could happen to be nearby — stuck in traffic, for instance. Jet-powered drones can reach Kyiv from Russia’s Bryansk region in half an hour, depending on the model, and can fly around the entire city in three or four minutes. In that situation, there’s nothing you can do.
Russia has also been attacking Ukrainian data centers recently. Take the strike on the National Academy of Sciences [on September 28]: One of the offices of Ukrtelecom, a Ukrainian internet provider, is in the building next door. That same day, there was a strike on another Ukrtelecom office, which shares a building with the private clinic Dobrobut. Another strike [on September 25] hit a data center in Shuliavka, in an office building. There were terrible scenes there, too — bodies were literally lying in the street.
Russia isn’t holding back — I’m saying that without exaggeration. It’s not necessarily setting out to strike civilian facilities in these particular cases, but this is no longer collateral damage. It’s part of the military strategy. Russia can strike a gas station or a large office complex during the workday. It apparently intends to stick with this tactic. And with everything flying so fast, you don’t even have time to do anything.
— You’ve already said that internet and communications services in general could soon get more expensive in Ukraine. Are people already feeling the effects of attacks on data centers? Has internet service in Kyiv gotten worse?
— There are local disruptions, yes. At one point, roughly 100,000 subscribers in Kyiv and the Kyiv region lost internet access. But I still find it hard to understand exactly what this campaign is meant to achieve. The military’s internet infrastructure isn’t entirely independent of these data centers, but they [the Ukrainian armed forces] have their own infrastructure and networks, plus Starlink. These attacks seem more aimed at the civilian economy. Ukraine relies heavily on digital services.
How effective are they really? You might find yourself unable to pay for something by card, but there won’t be a total catastrophe. Ukraine may have one of the most decentralized networks of internet providers in Europe, or even the world — there are about a thousand operators in the country. Of course, there are big companies, but overall it’s a very extensive network.
‘We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant’
— Are businesses managing to adapt to round-the-clock attacks and the changed conditions?
— It varies a lot. I’ve spoken with people running many large restaurants and food-service chains. They all have different views of the future, but they agree that restaurants in shopping malls won’t survive this winter: It’s dangerous to have employees come to work there during an air raid alert, even a yellow-level one.
There are reasons to believe Russia will strike shopping malls. So not only restaurants but probably all retail businesses in those malls will close down. And shopping malls are an important part of Ukraine’s economy. Kyiv has Respublika and Blockbuster Mall — they’re among the largest shopping malls in Ukraine and [Eastern] Europe.
Business owners — whether they sell clothing, run restaurants, or do something else — are trying to find solutions. But nobody can predict with complete certainty what things will look like in winter, so everyone’s improvising.
More generally, businesses are trying to adapt: A red alert means we don’t work; a yellow alert means we try to work somehow, because otherwise you could go crazy.
— Can a red alert last for hours?
— No, actually. That’s more likely with yellow alerts. This is a deliberate Russian tactic: launching small groups of jet-powered drones one after another. One arrives, gets shot down, then another is launched. It’s all done either to keep a yellow alert going almost indefinitely or to have another yellow alert issued 20 minutes later.
A red alert means either a truly massive drone attack or a specific missile threat.
— How much have Kyiv residents’ daily routines changed since attacks started happening during working hours?
— There is no routine — everyone’s improvising. Meetings are constantly being rescheduled and canceled, but businesses somehow manage to keep working. I’m amazed myself at how the cafés on my street manage to open on time. If you want to get a coffee at a café that opens at 8 a.m., somehow you can.
We’ve been through all sorts of things in four and a half years. But never this level of anxiety. Now it’s constant. People see it all happening. Very often, jet-powered Gerans fly right overhead. This will sound surprising, but that’s a good thing, because it means you won’t be directly hit. Most likely.
I’ve seen a lot over these years, but when this superfast thing that sounds like a quiet jet aircraft races over your head, it really gets to you.
— How has life changed for families with children?
— Everything’s become harder for them, because the children are effectively learning remotely all the time. Officially, it’s hybrid or in person, but the reality this school year is distance learning.
And this is another area where the internet situation matters. Because if attacks on energy infrastructure intensify, cell service and internet access could go down.
But the city has been through that before.
— The daily attacks must also have affected hospitals. How are they operating now?
— As a rule, surgery doesn’t stop during an alert — it all depends on the specific situation. During a red alert, hospitals try to move anyone they can to a shelter. During a yellow alert, they’re more likely to keep patients where they are, and 80% of Kyiv’s air raid alerts are yellow. Nobody moves intensive care patients anywhere. Ambulances and intensive care units keep working all the time.
As for strikes on hospitals, I wouldn’t say hospitals are being deliberately targeted at this point. But honestly, with the current strategy of terror — let’s call it that — we can’t rule out Russia moving on to that. Take the strike on the private clinic Dobrobut: The clinic wasn’t the specific target. Though perhaps Russia didn’t mind it getting hit, either.
There could be serious problems with medicines in the future. Some medications could be in short supply: There have been strikes on a facility in Kyiv belonging to Darnytsia, a major pharmaceutical company. This is primarily part of the economic war, but attacks like these show that Russia doesn’t care much about civilian lives. I don’t think that needs explaining anymore in 2026.
There’s also collateral damage. When warehouses are attacked, absolutely everyone gets hit — book publishers, manufacturers of all kinds of things. Quite a few warehouses storing medicines have also been destroyed. That doesn’t mean there’ll be a catastrophe, but shortages of certain medicines could develop.
You can support Ukrainian civilians facing these difficult conditions through Davayte, a project launched by Meduza, Helpdesk, and TV Rain in February 2024. We collect donations and work with our partners to help Ukrainians repair their homes and recover from injuries caused by Russian attacks, provide shelter for people who have lost their homes, and much more. Please follow this link to find out how to donate quickly and securely.
‘Shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable’
— You mentioned that Russia is heavily attacking warehouses in Ukraine. In late August, Agriculture and Food Minister Taras Vysotskyi said that about 90% of the country’s grocery-chain warehouses had been destroyed. Can you see that in the selection of products in stores?
— Yes, it’s changing. That’s especially true of perishables, because there are virtually no refrigerated warehouses left in the Kyiv region [because of Russian attacks].
I can’t say we’re facing an across-the-board shortage of fish, meat, or milk. But the selection has shrunk, and exactly what’s missing from stores depends directly on what was damaged two, three, or four days earlier. For example, right now you can barely find cola in Kyiv supermarkets, because the Coca-Cola plant in Brovary was hit very recently.
I don’t think there’s a risk of famine. Ukraine’s agricultural sector has enormous capacity, despite all the problems of 2022. But shortages and major price increases are almost inevitable. We can’t yet tell how severe they’ll be. But you’ll certainly be able to get through the winter eating, say, buckwheat.
There’s an effort now to reorganize logistics so that more goods go straight from suppliers to supermarkets. But the vehicle fleets that retail chains and suppliers needed and maintained in the 2000s no longer exist.
There’s still the option of importing food from the EU. We saw a similar situation in 2022 with gasoline and food. Back then, Russia was destroying Ukraine’s few oil refineries, and now Ukraine depends almost entirely on gasoline from Europe.
— In August, Ukrainian media reported that air raid alerts were bringing Kyiv’s transportation system to a standstill. The metro had effectively stopped carrying passengers, and buses and trolleybuses were overcrowded. Kyiv residents were flagging down cars in the street and asking drivers to give them a ride to the other bank. How is public transportation working now?
— That was actually one of the reasons for dividing alerts into yellow and red levels. All city-run surface transportation keeps operating during yellow alerts. That’s dangerous, of course, but otherwise the city simply can’t function.
Previously, though, large numbers of passengers on buses and trolleybuses would be made to get off at the nearest stop. If you can’t get to a shelter, that’s hardly safe, either.
The metro is a little different. Kyiv has three lines, two of which connect the left and right banks. During yellow alerts, one of those stops running, and the other becomes severely overcrowded.
— Has planning a route become harder?
— I’d strongly recommend avoiding trips from one bank to the other whenever possible. Especially from the left bank to the right. The city center is on the right bank, so large numbers of people travel there for work in the morning and return in the evening.
That’s another reason so many people are being switched to remote work. There’s the general safety concern, but also a very specific everyday problem: With constant traffic jams, people can easily be an hour late. There’s no point sitting in traffic.
— Since the beginning of October, the Russian military has struck bridges over the Dnipro several times, particularly the Northern and Southern bridges. What consequences could those attacks have for the city?
— Completely destroying bridges over the Dnipro is virtually impossible — we can see that from many other bridges in Ukraine. Despite continuing attacks and damage, the bridge over the Dniester estuary in Zatoka [in the Odesa region], the bridge over the Dnipro in Zaporizhzhia, and the Antonivskyi Bridge in Kherson are all still standing. Ukrainian forces struck the Antonivskyi Bridge during their counteroffensive in the fall of 2022, when Kherson was still occupied.
We’re talking about strategically important bridges, not small structures somewhere on the Siverskyi Donets, which really can be destroyed.
Still, if intensive attacks on Kyiv’s bridges continue, serious logistical problems will naturally develop. According to Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, roughly 600,000 vehicles cross Kyiv’s main bridges every day.
The city is now considering setting up pontoon crossings and ferries, but as I understand it, the infrastructure needed for that isn’t ready yet. And it would be hard to replace the Southern Bridge fully that way, for example. It’s particularly important for transportation and logistics: A significant share of freight passing through the capital crosses it, and it also carries a metro line.
‘A friend of mine says she’s learned to fall asleep in the metro without worrying about what might happen’
— You regularly see headlines about air raid alerts lasting for hours. According to Ukrainska Pravda, Kyiv had one of its longest air raid alerts on September 28: It lasted more than nine hours. How does the city change during an air attack?
— It depends. If you walk around Kyiv during an ordinary attack, when there aren’t explosions right around you — whether you’re downtown or elsewhere — the city won’t look much different from normal. Life doesn’t stop. It’s an ordinary workday: People go about their business, drink coffee, and go places.
When there’s a confirmed threat of ballistic missile strikes, things are a little different. You can see people trying either to take cover with two walls between them and the outside or to get to a shelter. Again, it varies from person to person and depends on where you are.
What has really changed is that quite a few people, including people I know, are choosing to spend every night in a shelter — in the metro or an underground parking garage, for example. For many, that’s hard mentally, but a friend of mine, for instance, says she’s learned to fall asleep without worrying about what might happen.
Signs of a massive combined strike — an attack involving cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, and drones — usually appear several hours [before the strike itself]. You can tell whether an attack is coming from the movements of strategic bombers inside Russia.
At times like that, Kyiv’s metro is packed. The record for the number of people spending the night in the metro has been broken many times. The current record is 56,000. Realistically, that’s the maximum the metro can accommodate. Experts give higher figures, but after this summer’s combined attacks, you get the impression those are only possible on paper.
— Does Kyiv have enough shelters? Are they equipped for attacks lasting hours?
— The situation is pretty bad. Kyiv has about 4,500 shelters. It’s hard to say whether that’s a lot or a little. Not all of them are in good condition, and, let’s put it this way, not all of them are actually accessible.
During a jet-powered drone attack, conventional shelters — the metro, basements in schools and government buildings, and so on — aren’t all that helpful. They’re important, but Kyiv has almost none of what you see in Kharkiv and Odesa, for example. There, you can see portable concrete shelters on the streets that provide decent protection from drones.
Why are there almost none in Kyiv? That’s partly down to domestic politics. I don’t want to get too deep into it, but President Zelensky and Mayor Klitschko have been at odds for a long time. Different authorities block each other’s decisions to some extent.
I don’t want to take anyone’s side. But why almost nothing has been done about portable shelters in four years remains an open question. Kyiv’s mayor bears a great deal of responsibility here.
— What’s happening in Kyiv’s shelters during these hours-long alerts?
— Sometimes in the evenings, people try to get [into the stations] before the metro closes so they can lay out their mattresses and other things. Sometimes there’s a fight for spots.
Apart from these rather comical situations, I don’t think the atmosphere is that bad. It probably doesn’t compare anymore with the start of the war, when people held impromptu concerts in the stations. But even though everyone’s on edge, you can still feel people supporting each other. They share coffee and sandwiches, get to know each other, and so on.
Several times, I’ve gone down into the metro specifically as a journalist, to see how it all works and how people behave. And you really can still see some of that unity.
— In September, the Kyiv Post reported that Kyiv residents were increasingly ignoring air raid warnings. What do you think about that?
— You have to understand that it’s impossible to respond to every air raid alert for four and a half years. At some point, you could just go crazy. During yellow alerts, you could theoretically spend 18 hours in a shelter, but, as you can imagine, almost nobody does that.
But at night, when the chance of a ballistic missile strike is fairly high, people do go to shelters. I’d say that since May 2026, there’s actually been a noticeable increase in the number of Kyiv residents who don’t ignore air raid alerts.
‘People who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time’
— You’ve already mentioned attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. Last year, some districts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks at a time, and temperatures often dropped below minus 20 degrees Celsius (minus 4 degrees Fahrenheit). What’s the outlook for this winter?
— It’s obvious there’ll be problems with energy supplies. Russia is trying to cut Kyiv off from the country’s power grid by striking both thermal power plants and power lines. Frequent repeat attacks make it harder to repair the damage. Kyiv could end up spending a week or two either with no electricity at all or with power for just a few hours a day. Hospitals, public and private, have long been ready for this. They largely prepared during the first winter of the war: They have generators and fuel reserves, so things are more or less okay on that front.
Air defense is also in worse shape now, for the reasons I mentioned at the beginning. But the weather is expected to be better this winter. Electricity consumption has also fallen. I think this winter will be more or less like the last one. It won’t be good, but I’m not expecting an outright apocalypse.
There could be problems with the sewer system — that’s very dangerous, and you can’t really prepare for it. If that happens, it’ll be a new experience for Kyiv residents.
— Last year, 600,000 people left Kyiv because of power and heating outages. Should we expect a similar mass exodus this winter?
— First, I want to point out that Klitschko’s figure of 600,000 was pulled out of thin air. People did leave, but there wasn’t a noticeable exodus. This winter will probably be different, since a whole range of factors will come into play.
Obviously, for people who have relatives [in other cities] or a house in some village where they can at least heat with firewood, that’s an option. But many people’s ability to travel is limited — primarily, I’m talking about military mobilization. There are checkpoints outside Kyiv, and if your paperwork isn’t all in order, you won’t get very far by car. So some people effectively won’t be able to leave Kyiv. And their girlfriends, wives, and children often stay with them.
And as I’ve already said, prices have risen so much that many people can’t afford to rent an apartment somewhere in western Ukraine.
— Can those who stay in the city prepare for winter?
— There’s nothing new here. Obviously, you can’t put a gasoline generator on the balcony of an apartment building, because your whole apartment could burn down. But people generally already have their power banks, EcoFlow portable power stations, and all that equipment ready.
I’m not saying everyone does, because there are people who don’t put much effort into it and just take things as they come. But people who wanted to prepare for winter have mostly been ready for a long time.

Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy also responded to the Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight, saying Moscow has used “more than a hundred different weapons,” from “jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles.”

Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. Zelenskyy also says Ukraine has halted strikes on Russian oil refineries for two days after Trump’s ceasefire announcement, but “Russia did not heed the American president.”
“During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine. Nineteen regions of our country have come under attack in these two days alone.

Global pressure on Russia contributes to exactly that – bringing peace closer. “This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he wrote on social media. He did not apportion blame for the lack of warning, calling it unfortunate.
US officials made explicit threats over the weekend to their Ukrainian counterparts that the Trump administration was on the brink of halting intelligence sharing with Kyiv.
However, speaking in Warsaw, Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, indicated that cooperation was continuing and said the lack of warning over the Kyiv attack was due to a “special type” of Russian weaponry.
Donald Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.
He also claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me”. On Tuesday Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.
The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said. “Russia did not heed the president … The Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted.
Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.

Sam Jones
in Madrid
The Spanish lawyer Miriam González Durántez has launched a new liberal, centrist party, vowing to clean up politics and give voters an alternative to the dominant socialist and conservative parties as the country gears up for next month’s snap general election.
González Durántez, an ex-EU adviser who is married to the former British deputy prime minister Nick Clegg, says her new party, Democracia21, will offer a modern, transparent kind of politics that “doesn’t feed on fear, insults or nostalgia”.
Democracia21’s manifesto accuses both the ruling Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) and the rightwing People’s party (PP) of squandering decades of government for short-term political ends.
“In the meantime: housing became unaffordable, young people left, bureaucracy grew like a religion, and bickering took the place of governing,” it says.

Same-sex couple sue over Slovakia’s refusal to register marriage
Rob Cameron
A same-sex couple are suing authorities in Slovakia for refusing to register their Austrian marriage, testing whether a landmark EU court ruling can turn recognition abroad into legal security at home.
Their fight exposes a clash between European obligations and national restrictions – and what that means for LGBTQ+ people living under Robert Fico’s populist-nationalist government.
Ivan Novotný, 31, and Metod Špaček, 51, married in Austria in 2020, but six years on, their marital status at home remains unrecognised.
There is no same-sex marriage in Slovakia, a socially conservative, predominantly Catholic country; neither is there any form of civil partnership.
But Novotný and Špaček, who are both lawyers and former diplomats, are not asking for that. They want the Slovakian authorities to recognise a marriage that was concluded legally in another EU country – something the bloc’s top court has said is mandatory for all EU members.
The couple argue they are on solid legal ground after a ruling by the EU’s highest court in November 2025 in response to a case brought by a Polish same-sex couple who had married in Berlin.

He added that such a deal “funds Putin’s war” against Ukraine.
The Finnish prime minister urged Europe and Ukraine’s supporters to “say this forcefully to Trump”.
“Continuing support for Ukraine is now more essential than ever,” he added.

She said this summer’s huge border crossing of migrants from Morocco into Ceuta – in which about 140 people are estimated to have died – showed just how quickly “sudden massive arrivals can put pressure on the EU’s external borders”.
Her proposals include broadening the powers of the EU’s border agency, Frontex, including a new “Quick Reaction Force for crisis deployment”, and increasing the bloc’s return rate.
The European Parliament in June approved an overhaul of migration policy aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish centres abroad, in what critics warned could weaken safeguards for asylum seekers.

Dombrovskis said:
As regards specifically this question on Russian diesel exports, if we look at the volumes, they are not of any macroeconomic significance, and frankly, there are strong doubts whether Russia is even able to supply those volumes, and according also to US quality standards, those are big question marks.

articles.title: Russian Rassvet satellite system threatens Ukraine, Europe and global security – Maj Gen Pavlenko
articles.body:
The Russian Rassvet satellite network is being developed not only for the war against Ukraine, but also as a tool for carrying out provocations, illegal schemes, and hybrid aggression against NATO countries and the international community, Deputy Chief of the Main Intelligence Agency of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense from 2015 to 2020, Major General Illia Pavlenko said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine.
According to Pavlenko, the creation of an autonomous satellite infrastructure will allow Russia to covertly carry out sabotage operations anywhere in the world.
"This is a direct threat to Europeans. The enemy is moving its jet-powered UAV production facilities underground. Equipped with a compact Rassvet terminal, such a drone, launched from a civilian vessel in the English Channel or from a rented trailer in Europe, will be able to strike targets in London or Paris unhindered, guided directly from the Kremlin. Europe simply won't have enough expensive PAC-3 missiles for the Patriot system to repel massive attacks by cheap satellite-guided drones," the major general said.
Pavlenko identifies Russia's plans to sell network access in 70 countries of the Global South as a separate risk. "Somali pirates will undoubtedly use this connection to guide unmanned boats toward civilian vessels, and drug cartels in Latin America will use it to circumvent U.S. surveillance systems. Giving them such a tool is effectively like giving an enemy nuclear weapons," he said.
In addition, the general noted that the Russian developers of Rassvet have chosen an operating frequency band that completely overlaps with the frequencies of the American Iridium satellite system used by the Pentagon, creating a risk of interference and complicating the use of electronic warfare (EW) capabilities.
"This is a major threat to the Americans and NATO countries. By jamming Rassvet's frequencies in the event of a hybrid conflict or the fight against smuggling, they risk completely crippling their own communications and the command and control of their warships or units," a former high-ranking military intelligence official said.

articles.title: Iran fortifies nuclear sites, prepares for renewed war: report
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran fortifies nuclear sites as it prepares for renewed US war: report
Iran is strengthening its nuclear and military facilities, mobilising supporters and threatening a wider regional conflict as it prepares for the possibility of renewed war with the United States, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal.
Iranian leaders believe US President Donald Trump could launch fresh attacks after the 3 November midterm elections, prompting Tehran to reinforce sensitive sites and warn Washington that another offensive would trigger a more devastating response, the newspaper reported on Tuesday.
Citing Iranian officials and people familiar with regional communications, the WSJ said Tehran had issued both public and private warnings that renewed US strikes could lead to attacks on American interests and Gulf allies.
Satellite imagery has shown Iran strengthening defences around nuclear facilities and border areas, while authorities have stepped up pro-government rallies and promoted military training for civilians.
Iran's limited ability to counter advanced US fighter jets, high-altitude bombers and cruise missiles has pushed Tehran to rely increasingly on threats of wider retaliation to deter Washington, according to the report.
Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at London-based Chatham House, said the prospect of war also served Iran's leadership as it grappled with diplomatic, economic and political deadlock.
Iran threatens Gulf infrastructure and US warships
Iranian officials have raised the possibility of launching ground incursions into neighbouring countries in response to further US attacks, according to people familiar with Tehran's warnings.
Senior Iranian national security official Mohsen Rezaei warned on Sunday that the United Arab Emirates could be targeted, along with regional data centres and internet cables.
Tehran has also warned Arab officials that critical infrastructure, including Saudi oil facilities, could come under attack if fighting resumes, the WSJ reported.
The threats come as Saudi Arabia faces mounting attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's airport on Saturday killed at least 13 people and wounded hundreds, according to the newspaper, which described it as the deadliest attack on the US or its Gulf allies during the conflict linked to the war with Iran.
Iran has also told intermediaries that it could respond more forcefully against American military personnel, including by attempting to sink US warships and inflict casualties among their crews.
The warnings highlight the risks to the Gulf's vital economic infrastructure if Trump orders another round of strikes.
US sends more military assets to Middle East
The US military is also preparing for a possible resumption of hostilities, with a third aircraft carrier strike group and an additional Marine unit heading towards the region according to the outlet.
The Pentagon is considering sending more air defence systems and ammunition to American bases across the region.
Trump ruled out launching an attack before the midterm elections last week but publicly raised the possibility of striking Iran's Mount Pickaxe nuclear site.
US officials said the military was developing several options for renewed strikes.
Direct fighting between Washington and Tehran has eased considerably since late July, when Trump backed away from plans for a major escalation, partly over concerns about dwindling interceptor missile stocks needed to protect American and regional targets.
The lull has nevertheless allowed both sides to prepare for another confrontation.
Iran has used the period to rebuild missile and drone production facilities and replenish its weapons stockpiles, while Washington has intensified economic pressure on Tehran.
Meanwhile, attacks on commercial shipping and tankers in the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz have increased.
At least three merchant vessels came under attack over the weekend, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency.
A drone strike on the Emirati tanker Petro Dolphin near Oman on Sunday sparked a fire aboard the vessel and left two Indian sailors missing.
Iran reinforces nuclear sites and mobilises civilians
Satellite images taken by Vantor and analysed by the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security show Iran constructing new defensive barriers around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear facilities.
The measures, introduced last month, include makeshift earthworks designed to obstruct potential ground raids.
Iranian officials have also sought to demonstrate the country's readiness for another war.
Brigadier General Gholamreza Jalali, who oversees Iran's contingency planning, said in late September that airports, seaports and power plants had been equipped with shelters and emergency supplies to maintain operations during a conflict.
State media have meanwhile intensified coverage of pro-government demonstrations, with residents reporting that rallies have grown larger and spread to more locations in recent weeks.
Billboards in Tehran have advertised civilian training courses in the use of shoulder-fired anti-aircraft missiles and sniper rifles.
Last month, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps released footage of women undergoing training in guerrilla warfare, firearms and drone operations through its Basij paramilitary force.
In the northeastern city of Sabzevar, Revolutionary Guard personnel visited a kindergarten to recount stories of earlier fighting and display a US-made Tomahawk missile they claimed to have intercepted.
Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran programme at the Washington-based Foundation for Defense of Democracies, said Tehran's political rhetoric and military preparations indicated it was actively preparing for another confrontation.
He described the measures as serving both deterrence and war planning.

articles.title: What is known about West providing Ukraine with no intel on Russian missile launches
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Ukrainian air defense systems were unable to intercept Russian ballistic missiles in time due to a lack of necessary data from Kiev’s Western partners, Ukrainian air force spokesman Yury Ignat said.
Vladimir Zelensky later confirmed this information.
TASS has summarized the key facts about the situation.
Lack of data
- Ukrainian air defense systems were unable to respond to Russian ballistic missile launches in time due to a lack of necessary data from Kiev’s Western partners, Ukrainian air force spokesman Yury Ignat said.
- He blamed the shortfall on "technical issues," noting that this was not the first time such an incident had occurred.
- Earlier, the Ukrainian air force confirmed that the country’s air defenses had been unable to receive data on Russian ballistic missile launches in time, adding that the ballistic targets were only detected by radar systems as the attack on Kiev was underway.
- The Ukrainian air force also said that the cause of the incident was being determined.
- On the evening of October 12, Ukrainian media reported that explosions were heard in Kiev before an air raid alert was issued.
- Later, Vladimir Zelensky said that Ukraine had not received intelligence from its partners before the overnight explosions.
- He called intelligence one of the most critical issues.
Possible reasons
- Ignat told the Rada television channel that specialists would investigate the incident and coordinate with Western partners to resolve the problem.
- Meanwhile, Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation under the National Security and Defense Council said on its Telegram channel that it was looking into the reasons for the disruption in the transmission of intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches as various theories circulated online.
- The center noted that one possibility was that the transfer of intelligence to Ukraine had been suspended, although official details were still being verified.
- The European edition of Politico reported that US President Donald Trump could cut off US intelligence to Ukraine or pressure entrepreneur Elon Musk to disconnect Starlink satellite internet, on which the Ukrainian military depends heavily.
- The Financial Times newspaper reported, citing unnamed European officials, that the US administration was threatening to suspend the weapons procurement program and the provision of intelligence to Ukraine.
- Meanwhile, the Ukrainian news outlet Strana noted that there had been no official information confirming that the United States might have halted intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a defense industry museum displaying an intercontinental ballistic missile capable of reaching the United States, state media KCNA showed on Tuesday.
The report came a day after US President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia. Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in mid-November.

"The exhibition appears intended to highlight the achievements of Kim's defense science development program," Shin said. "It gave the impression of propaganda aimed at gaining a strategic advantage ahead of a potential North Korea-US summit."
North Korea shows off military developments
Analysts said the museum also reflected a broader effort by Kim to elevate North Korea's weapons displays into lasting symbols of the regime's military accomplishments.

Separately, North Korea said it test-fired a tactical ballistic missile on Monday to confirm the successful technical upgrade of an unspecified key component.

articles.title: Whitaker Says ‘No Change’ to Arms Flows to Kyiv via PURL
articles.body:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker said, to his knowledge, US weapon flows to Kyiv via NATO continue as of Monday.
Speaking to AFP on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday, Whitaker said he was unaware of any changes to the existing supply structure.

“The United States continues to sell our equipment and munitions to our European and Canadian allies that then provide it to Ukraine,” Whitaker said.
“I know of no change to that program.”
Whitaker referred to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) mechanism, where alliance members bankroll US weaponry for Kyiv.
The comments followed a Financial Times (FT) report on Sunday, citing unnamed European officials, that Washington is considering cutting arms flows via PURL over US President Donald Trump’s Friday diesel deal with Moscow.
The rumors stem from Kyiv’s hinted refusal to halt attacks on Russian refineries unless Washington secures a bilateral ceasefire that protects Ukraine’s energy grid, with the current terms, after Trump announced an energy truce, rumored to overwhelmingly favor Moscow by including only refineries.
Whitaker’s comments also echoed those of US Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich at the same event, who called for Europe to bolster arms supplies to Kyiv via PURL in response to Russia’s hybrid threats.
However, Whitaker also told AFP he did not wish to comment on “unconfirmed reports” without referencing the FT report.
Zelensky Says Ukraine Received No Warning From Partners Before Russian Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
Kyiv’s air defense challenges in winter
Whitaker also acknowledged the challenges Ukraine faces this winter, as Russia targets the country’s energy grid while Kyiv’s air defenses remain in short supply.
“Ukraine is facing a winter where, if there is not an energy ceasefire,... their electricity and heating infrastructure could be under a lot of pressure,” he said.
“Air defense largely is in high demand, and the availability is probably not as good as we would like,” he added.
Blackouts have already begun in Kyiv and other cities as the energy grid comes under attack. Strikes on Monday, one day after Trump boasted of an energy truce, also affected water supplies in Kyiv, less than two months before the arrival of subzero winter temperatures.
But Whitaker called it a “short-term challenge” as he said companies are coming up with alternatives to traditional air defense.
“You’re seeing a lot of companies try to come up with new and innovative ways to knock projectiles out of the air,” he said.
“Ultimately, we’re going to solve this problem… I think it’s a short-term challenge,” he added.
As Russia uses more jet-powered drones against Ukraine – with numbers spiking 10-fold from 350 in June to nearly 3,500 in September – Kyiv has also ostensibly explored more cost-effective ways to shoot down the drones.
Apart from using onboard 20mm autocannons from F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine also announced new models of faster interceptors to counter the jet-powered drones.
In Kyiv, automatic machine gun turrets are also being erected around the city after Russia began hitting the city’s bridges in October, with the Ukrainian Air Force hailing their successes in downing jet-powered drones.
But the quantity remains limited for now, and it’s unclear whether Kyiv can scale production enough to cope with the upcoming Russian onslaught this winter.

articles.title: “Now it’s your turn”: US envoys planned to show Moscow a refinery pause and a diesel deal, then ask for something back, a source tells Reuters
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump’s envoys told Kyiv that letting Russia sell diesel could draw Moscow back to peace talks, Reuters reported. In the same meeting, they said Russia’s leader was not ready to negotiate. Since then, Moscow has offered nothing in return, and Trump has brushed off claims that Russia helps Iran.
Washington is pressing Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries and offering Moscow economic incentives to return to peace talks, even though Russia has made no commitment in return. Yesterday, Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before air raid sirens sounded, amid disputed warnings that the US could cut intelligence support. Meanwhile, Ukraine is being asked to halt its long-range campaign against the oil infrastructure that fuels and finances Russia's war.
The pitch: a diesel deal as a signal to Moscow
Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner met the Ukrainian delegation in Miami on 9 October. They described Russian President Vladimir Putin as unprepared to negotiate but said the diesel deal could help restart three-way talks, two of the sources said.
The third source said the deal could “soften” Moscow because it “sends a signal that Trump is open to do things” with Russia. One of the sources described the plan:
“The idea was that the US could go back to Russia and say ‘See, the Ukrainians stopped striking and we gave you this deal. Now it’s your turn to do something.’”
Ukraine’s part was to stop hitting Russian refineries. Kushner repeated Trump’s request at the meeting, noting the administration had made it several times, two sources said.
EU blacklists 1,569 Russian arms suppliers and their bosses in its biggest sanctions round ever, as Trump eases up on Moscow
Kyiv was asked to hold its fire on Russian oil
The Ukrainians agreed to nothing formally, Reuters’ sources said. They signaled they would accept an energy ceasefire if Russia did the same, but saw the US approach as an attempt to appease Russia with business deals.
Two days later, Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready if Russia reciprocated. Three sources told Reuters the envoys did not threaten to cut US support over the refinery strikes. US officials are also believed to have told European allies that Trump would halt PURL, the NATO scheme for Europe-funded US weapons for Ukraine, unless the strikes stopped, according to FT.
Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly
What Moscow has offered in return
A person close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin would return to the table only when he gets “the remaining 11% of Donbas.” Ukraine refuses to cede more land. During the 9 October call that produced the deal, Putin declined to commit to resuming talks, his aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, Axios reported.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak, meanwhile, claimed diesel exports could reach 3.0–3.5 million tons a month by year-end, above the volumes Trump announced.
“Too much to lose”: Trump on Russia and Iran
Late on 12 October, Trump wrote on Truth Social that he did not believe Russia and China were helping Iran, since they have “too much to lose.” In March, he told Fox News that Putin “might be helping them a little bit.” Asked about Russia’s possible support for Iran, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on 2 September that his message to everyone was to “stay away.” That month, a Financial Times investigation found Russia secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles that could threaten US warships.

articles.title: NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
articles.body:

NATO Unveils “Theory of Victory” to Stop Russian Attack With Drones and Missiles
NATO has outlined a new defense strategy, dubbed the “Theory of Victory,,” designed to repel a potential Russian attack by halting its initial offensive, preventing further advances, and systematically weakening enemy forces.
According to The Wall Street Journal on October 12, NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, presented the strategy during the Warsaw Security Forum, revealing that its classified version had been finalized three months earlier.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Drawing on lessons from Ukraine’s battlefield experience, the strategy prioritizes investment in what Grynkewich called “affordable mass,” focusing on relatively low-cost drones to supplement NATO’s advanced weapons systems, according to the publication.
Under the plan, NATO’s immediate priority in the event of a Russian attack would be to stop the initial assault.
“Enemy formations will be starved of replenishment. Enemy commanders will be unable to control their forces. Enemy forces and support capabilities will be reduced and destroyed,” Grynkewich said.
The NATO commander emphasized that the Alliance’s objective would not be to defeat Russia as a state or undermine its government, but rather to repel any attack against NATO territory.
According to The Wall Street Journal, the strategy builds on earlier work by General Chris Donahue, a former commander of US Army forces in Europe and NATO’s Allied Land Command.
The approach is intended to address concerns that Russia’s geographical advantages and extensive defense industry could enable it to launch an offensive against the Baltic states, Poland, or other NATO members before the Alliance could organize a substantial military response.
A central element of the strategy involves establishing a large autonomous zone in which unmanned aerial vehicles and ground-based robotic systems would be deployed to disrupt and suppress Russian attacks while minimizing casualties among allied forces.
At the same time, NATO would use long-range missiles to strike Russian command centers and air defense systems in the Kaliningrad exclave, near St. Petersburg, and in Belarus. According to The Wall Street Journal, these operations would aim to weaken Russia’s ability to control the airspace, creating conditions for the US Army’s V Corps and other NATO ground forces to launch counterattacks.
NATO air forces would also move rapidly to target Russian reinforcements approaching the battlefield and strike additional military assets behind enemy lines.
The operations would be supported by a secure information-sharing network known as a “data backbone,” allowing NATO forces to exchange classified targeting data almost instantaneously through a cloud-based system. According to reports, components of the network have already been tested in the Middle East during the US war with Iran.
The broader concept, known as the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative, is intended to strengthen NATO’s ability to respond rapidly to potential Russian aggression.
According to US military officials cited by The Wall Street Journal, the initiative ultimately aims to deter Russian leader Vladimir Putin from launching an attack against the Alliance.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader shift toward integrating emerging technologies into military operations, particularly those that have demonstrated their effectiveness on Ukraine’s battlefield.
On August 12, Bild reported that NATO was increasingly prioritizing drones, satellite technology, advanced sensors, and artificial intelligence as part of its efforts to modernize its military capabilities.
The move toward greater automation draws on Ukraine’s experience deploying AI-powered drone swarms capable of identifying targets, coordinating their movements, and conducting strikes autonomously, even when Russian electronic warfare disrupts communication with human operators.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine trade accusations concerning overnight strikes that kill at least 4
articles.body:
Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed at least four people and injured over 60 others.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said in a statement on Telegram that three people were killed and 15 others injured when a Russian missile strike destroyed a section of a four-story residential building in the Kholodnohirskyi district of Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city.
The DSNS reported that the strike occurred on Monday evening and also targeted the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district, noting that four people were rescued, though some may still be trapped under the debris.
“Despite the threat of repeated strikes, rescue workers, police, medics, volunteers, K-9 units, and municipal crews are working at the scene,” the DSNS added.
The DSNS later updated the death toll to four and the number of injured to 41.
Meanwhile, the Kyiv City Military Administration said one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the Darnytskyi district.
Khmelnytskyi Governor Serhii Tiurin said four people were injured in the western region after drones targeted it over the past day, adding that the windows and entrance area of a regional medical facility were damaged during one of the attacks.
In the northwestern Rivne region, Governor Oleksandr Koval said 20 people were injured, one critically, in a strike on the regional capital that damaged an educational building.
Separately, Heorhii Reshetnikov, acting governor of the southern Mykolaiv region, said a cargo terminal and an unspecified number of warehouses were damaged in Russian strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country received no early warning from its partners about the strikes in Kyiv, and that it has not carried out strikes on Russia's energy sector in general for the two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a statement on US social media company X.
"Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war," he added.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed air defenses shot down 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight. It added that Russia launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles from the border region of Bryansk.
The Russian Defense Ministry, meanwhile, said it launched coordinated strikes against a workshop and locomotive depot in Kyiv, as well as a logistics center, a warehouse and dry cargo ship in the southern Mykolaiv region, which it said are “involved in delivering military cargo to Ukraine.”
Strikes in Russia
The ministry also claimed that air defenses shot down 604 Ukrainian drones over 15 regions and over the Sea of Azov.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin alleged that 417 drones were heading toward the region surrounding the Russian capital between 8.30 pm Monday (1730GMT) and 7 am Tuesday (0400GMT), with 65 of them destroyed.
Kaluga Governor Vladislav Shapsha said 73 drones were downed in his region overnight, damaging a school building, two private houses, and one car in the Mosalsky district.
The governors of the Tula and Voronezh regions reported Ukrainian drones being downed over their respective regions without any consequences, while Stavropol Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said damage was recorded in the industrial zone of the city of Nevinnomyssk.
“According to preliminary reports, there are no casualties, and there is no damage on the ground in Solnechnodolsk. … Inspections of the impact sites and damage assessments are ongoing, and repair work has begun,” Vladimirov said.
Yegor Kovalchuk, acting governor of the border region of Bryansk, said three firefighters were injured and hospitalized while extinguishing a blaze caused by a drone attack in the town of Zhukovka.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the war, which has been ongoing for more than four years.
Moscow and Kyiv have intensified strikes in recent months, targeting each other's logistics centers, ports, and energy infrastructure.
Both countries deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities only.
