Donald Trump has demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and has blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in fuel prices in the US. On Friday the US president announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia, dropping previous US sanctions.
He also claimed Moscow and Kyiv had agreed an “energy ceasefire”, something Zelenskyy described as “news to me”. On Tuesday Ukraine’s leader said his military had not struck Russian oil refineries or energy facilities in the two days following Trump’s Sunday announcement.
The Kremlin, however, had ignored the “ceasefire” and continued to bomb Ukraine’s energy infrastructure as before, with multiple attacks, he said. “Russia did not heed the president … The Russians sent absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes,” he noted.
Ukrainian commanders say American intelligence is not needed to identify targets for deep strikes on Russia, with oil refineries marked on Google Maps. But they say it plays a crucial role in warning of Russian ballistic missile launches, and the takeoff of long-range bomber aircraft.
In recent months Russia has dramatically stepped up its bombardment of Ukrainian towns and cities. Ukraine has struggled to shoot down incoming missiles and jet-powered drones and has appealed to partners to boost its dwindling supplies of US-made Patriot missiles.
According to the Financial Times, the Trump administration has also threatened to suspend the procurement scheme under which Ukraine’s European allies buy advanced US systems, which are then sent to Kyiv, including badly needed Patriots.
The Kremlin’s systematic campaign against Ukraine’s power grid has led to widespread blackouts in Kyiv and other cities. Putin’s apparent goal is to shut off heating and electricity for millions of civilians this winter, and to trigger a new wave of refugees into neighbouring EU states.
On Monday Russia bombarded the city of Kharkiv, destroying a residential building. Sharing footage from the scene, Zelenskyy said four people had been killed and 41 injured. Rescuers spent the entire night searching for people trapped under the rubble, he added.
The row between Washington and Kyiv is the most serious since last year, when Trump threw Zelenskyy out of the White House. Ukraine’s president has said he is willing to stop hitting Russian oil refineries – but only on a reciprocal basis and with “real guarantees” that Moscow will cease its attacks on Ukraine’s own energy sites.
“Direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying aid to Ukraine, and complicating protection of lives from ballistics – this is what will definitely not work for peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, strong partners are needed,” he said on Tuesday.

articles.title: Russian strike collapses a Kharkiv apartment stairwell and kills three, days after the US waived sanctions on Russia’s diesel
articles.body:
Russian munitions brought down a stairwell of an apartment building in Kharkiv on the evening of 12 October, and rescuers recovered three bodies from the rubble overnight, local authorities reported. Survivors described fire, falling glass, and pets left behind. The strike came days after Washington waived sanctions on Russian diesel, as it expects Kyiv to stop hitting Russian refineries.
Russia hits Ukraine’s cities every day as it readies a winter campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure, and its oil exports keep bringing in the money that pays for the drones and missiles. A halt to Ukraine’s refinery strikes with no matching halt to Russia’s strikes would leave Moscow’s fuel income intact while Kharkiv digs through rubble. Estonia’s prime minister has already urged Europe to help Ukraine destroy those refineries instead.
A stairwell gone in Kholodnohirskyi district
Russian munitions hit Kharkiv’s Kholodnohirskyi district repeatedly from around 21:17, and Mayor Ihor Terekhov preliminarily identified them as Banderols. At 22:21, he said one strike had hit a residential building, possibly trapping people. He then added in a follow-up post: “Very serious destruction—an entire stairwell has collapsed.”
The strike destroyed an entrance of the four-story building, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. It counted 11 injured across the city’s evening strikes, and a rescuer was hospitalized, while Terekhov put the number at 10. By 06:56 on 13 October, rescuers had found a third body. Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov confirmed three dead and said the search continued. Experts will check whether the building is still fit to live in, he added.
Over 24 hours, Russian attacks killed three people in Kharkiv and injured 37, including two children treated for acute stress, Syniehubov reported.
“I realize I’m on fire”: two residents recall the strike
Larysa Maksimenko had just put her bedridden husband to sleep when the strike hit, she told Suspilne Kharkiv. She suffered a head wound and burns.
“I went to the kitchen to switch on the kettle for myself, to have some coffee. I realize I’m on fire. Then glass fell on me. I came to, and I’m buried under everything. All covered in blood,” she said.
The window bars were broken, and medics carried her husband out through the window. Rescuers later found a woman under the rubble in her apartment, likely a neighbor, Maksimenko said. All she wants now, she said, is to get to her husband in hospital.
Viacheslav Chibitko, who lives on the second floor next to the collapsed entrance, saw a flash, and then everything blew out. He got his three dogs out, but five cats are still inside. During the clearing, a concrete slab fell on a rescuer, Suspilne’s correspondent reported. Crews pulled him out and handed him to medics.
Kyiv’s toll rises, and strikes hit other cities overnight
The evening drone strike on a 25-story building in Kyiv’s Darnytskyi district killed two people, Kyiv prosecutors reported. The second victim was found dead in a car near the building. Prosecutors counted at least seven injured, including a 17-year-old girl, while Mayor Vitali Klitschko counted 11 in the capital.
Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv before sirens, gap that lands hard amid fears that Washington could cut data that warns of launches
From 18:00 on 12 October, Russia launched five ballistic missiles, nine loitering munitions, and 108 attack drones, Ukraine’s Air Force reported. Air defenses downed or suppressed 88 drones. A Russian drone attack injured four patients at a medical facility in Khmelnytskyi Oblast, oblast head Serhii Tiurin said. In Dnipro, a Russian attack injured a 64-year-old man, oblast head Oleksandr Hanzha reported. A downed Russian drone set two houses on fire in Murovane near Lviv, oblast head Maksym Kozytskyi said.
On 12 October, a Russian Smerch rocket with a cluster warhead hit a house in Cherkaske, Donetsk Oblast, killing three people, including a 13-year-old girl, oblast head Vadym Filashkin reported.
Russian attacks killed more than 150 people in the week to 11 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russian bombs killed at least 20 people in Zaporizhzhia on 10 October, by the oblast’s count. On 9 October, the US waived its sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027. The White House expects Kyiv to halt refinery strikes under its proposed energy ceasefire.

articles.title: Trump slams ‘radical lunatics’ over claims Russia and China aid Iran
articles.body:
Trump slams ‘radical lunatics’ over claims Russia and China aid Iran
Russia and China are not likely to be providing assistance to Iran in its conflict with the US and Israel because they have “too much to lose,” US President Donald Trump has said. He dismissed allegations that the two countries are supporting Tehran, insisting that Washington would quickly detect any significant involvement.
The remarks come as US officials and Western media outlets claim that Russia and China are providing military and intelligence assistance to Iran, despite both countries calling for an end to the conflict.
In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump lashed out at political opponents he accused of spreading claims that Russia and China are helping Iran, while acknowledging that limited assistance cannot be ruled out.
“I see so many comments from the Radical Left Morons and Lunatics that China and Russia are helping the ‘wonderful’ Islamic Republic of Iran,” Trump wrote.
“If they are, it’s at a very low level, but I don’t believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast!” he added.
Trump’s statement follows earlier claims by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth that Russia and China are helping Iran in different ways. Speaking at a Senate hearing in July, Hegseth said both countries were “at different levels, enabling some of the things Iran is doing,” but declined to elaborate, citing classified information.
Joint Chiefs Chairman General Dan Caine also refused to discuss the extent of any involvement, saying it would reveal sensitive US intelligence.
Washington has sanctioned Chinese companies accused of supplying the Iranian military. In June, the US Treasury targeted Chinese- and Hong Kong-based firms allegedly involved in procuring weapons for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Defense Ministry.
Further sanctions in July targeted entities in China, Russia, and elsewhere accused of supporting an Iranian airline linked to weapons shipments.
The Wall Street Journal also reported that Chinese entities supplied Iran with satellite imagery, dual-use electronics, and components used in missiles and drones. China has denied providing military assistance to Iran.
Trump’s remarks follow a series of high-level contact with Moscow and Beijing focused on energy and economic cooperation.
At a meeting in September with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, Trump discussed Iran, trade, and energy, urging Beijing to boost refined fuel production to help stabilize global markets.
On Friday, Trump struck a diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease soaring fuel prices, after his administration repeatedly urged Kiev to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
The US subsequently eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 2027. Moscow pledged to supply 300,000 tons in October, 500,000 in November, and 1 million in December. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak said monthly shipments could eventually reach 3 million tons, with Russia lifting its export restrictions ahead of schedule.

Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before five Russian ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, stressing that intelligence on ballistic launches is one of the most critical tools for getting civilians to safety in time.
Russia launched more than 100 aerial weapons against Ukraine from the evening into the following day, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy wrote on X on October 13.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.

Kharkiv was among the hardest-hit cities. A Russian strike destroyed an apartment building, prompting an overnight rescue operation as emergency workers searched through the rubble. Four people were killed and 41 others injured in the city, according to Zelenskyy.
“An ordinary residential building was destroyed in Kharkiv; the rescue operation continued virtually all night as first responders searched for people under the rubble. Four people were killed in this strike on the building in Kharkiv. My condolences to all their families and loved ones,” he said.

The Ukrainian leader emphasized that advance intelligence is especially important during ballistic missile attacks because of the extremely short flight time, which leaves civilians and air defense crews only minutes to react.

articles.title: Iran may be digging in for next war, raising stakes for US, Israel and Gulf allies - analysis
articles.body:
Satellite images show that Iran is fortifying various locations as it may be preparing for renewed war, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.
“Iran is fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against the US and its Gulf allies as it prepares for potential American attacks after the midterms and seeks to deter them,” the article noted.
This comes amid a flurry of other reports suggesting that the US or Israel could return to fighting Iran.
Maariv said over the weekend that the United States had pressured Israel to carry out strikes against Iran. Both Israel and the US have upcoming elections. Any strikes could affect the elections.
PBS reported on Sunday that “Iran has continued to reject a deal with the US. The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States ‘insufficient’ as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along.”
The picture being painted is of an Iran that continues attempting to rebuild its missile and drone program.
Netanyahu said Iran can no longer produce ballistic missiles
In March, Israel’s prime minister said that the Islamic Republic could no longer produce ballistic missiles due to its hammering by US and Israeli strikes. There was also an optimistic assessment about how many Iranian launchers had been destroyed and how many missiles were “corked” in their depots by collapsing routes to the missiles.
In April, The New York Times reported that Iran was repairing its missile bunkers. The regime has shown it can rebuild capabilities.
The WSJ report noted that “Iran has also reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. Last month, it built passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces, according to Vantor satellite images analyzed by the Institute for Science and International Security, a Washington, DC, nonprofit.”
The report quoted Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. “In both word and deed, the Islamic Republic is actively preparing for the next war,” Ben Taleblu said.
Iran is a huge country, around 75 times the size of Israel and 150 times the size of Lebanon. Israel has struggled to defeat Hezbollah in Lebanon and remove all its threats. This illustrates the challenge of locating all the Iranian threats. The new report at the WSJ is concerning in this respect.
“Satellite images show Iran is strengthening sensitive locations, including nuclear sites and border areas, to make them more resilient to attacks. The government is also preparing Iranians for renewed war, sending paramilitary forces to read war stories to kindergartners, advertising training in firing shoulder-mounted anti-aircraft missiles, and holding rallies,” the report added.
It also said that Iran is prepared to defend against various types of airstrikes. It has likely learned some lessons from the 12 Day War in June 2025, as well as the round of strikes that began in February 2026 and lasted until May.
Iran continues to threaten shipping via the Strait of Hormuz. The US has been working to make sure that ships can pass the Strait. It is trying to make sure that the crisis with Iran doesn’t affect energy prices too much. However, all the levers the US has tried to pull still leave the conflict with Iran as an open-ended problem.
The WSJ noted that “Iranian officials have hinted that their forces could conduct land incursions into neighboring countries, according to people familiar with the warnings.”
With US forces having withdrawn from Iraq on September 30, this could give Iran some opportunities. It could try to infiltrate via Iraq or use Iranian-backed militias in Iraq to conduct more attacks. Those militias have already attacked a key pipeline in Saudi Arabia.
While US Central Command (CENTCOM) and Saudi Arabia carried out retaliatory strikes in July, there is reticence in Riyadh to confront the militias in Iraq and the Houthis at the same time.
Could renewed strikes produce different results?
This is why the WSJ report is important. It notes that “Tehran has separately warned Arab officials that it could strike regional targets, including Saudi oil facilities, in the event of a renewed conflict, some of the people said.”
Saudi Arabia is already weighing how to deal with the Houthi threat, which has targeted Saudi airports in recent days, killing and wounding people.
The question now is whether a return to fighting by the US or Israel will lead to better results than in the past.
Iran is seeking to rebuild; this means increasing its drone arsenal as well. The regime has had some success in attacking US bases in the region. It can read the same media reports as everyone else about how those attacks damaged facilities and airplanes and caused the US to reposition assets.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine did not receive early warning from partners on overnight strikes in Kyiv
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that his country did not receive an early warning from its partners on overnight Russian strikes on the capital Kyiv.
In a statement on US social media company X, Zelenskyy claimed that over 100 different weapons were used in overnight strikes by Russia, including ballistic missiles, hitting civilian infrastructure.
“Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said.
Commenting on an energy ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv announced by US President Donald Trump, Zelenskyy said Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or on the country’s energy sector in general for the two days since the announcement.
“But Russia did not heed the American President. During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine,” Zelenskyy added.
He said Ukraine’s readiness for “reciprocal steps toward de-escalation” has not changed, arguing “effective” pressure on Russia is needed for de-escalation, and that wars end “when the aggressor realizes that it cannot prolong the war.”
“Global pressure on Russia contributes to exactly that – bringing peace closer. But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed,” he added.
The Kyiv City Military Administration said in a separate Telegram statement that one person was injured in a strike that affected a residential building in the capital’s Darnytskyi district, as Ukraine claimed downing 88 out of 108 drones launched by Russia overnight.
In a statement, the country’s Air Force added that Moscow launched five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles against Ukraine from the Russian border region of Bryansk.
Separately, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told a panel of the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland that Kyiv continues to receive intelligence data from the US.
“Yes, we continue this cooperation (with the American side). And, also, it is true that yesterday’s attack, or night attack, (the) air raid alert was launched with a delay. But it is because of (the) special type of the weaponry which was used by (the) Russian side,” Sybiha said.
The Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, reported over the weekend that US envoys, in talks with their Ukrainian counterparts on Friday, raised the possibility of cutting off intelligence sharing to Kyiv if it did not heed Washington’s warning to halt energy strikes in Russia.

articles.title: 'They have too much to lose': Trump says he does not think China, Russia are helping Iran 'at all'
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said late on Monday he did not believe that China and Russia were helping Iran "at all," adding that Moscow and Beijing had "too much to lose" if they enabled Tehran.
Trump said on Truth Social that he had seen comments from his critics and opponents that China and Russia were helping Iran.
"If they are, it's at a very low level, but I don't believe they are at all. They have too much to lose, and we would know about it, and know about it very fast," Trump wrote.
Trump said in July he trusted China and Russia not to help Tehran in the Iran war, but warned that if they did get involved "it would be very bad for them."
The United States and Iran have been at war since February 28 when the US and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have since killed thousands and displaced millions.
Trump downplays China, Russia ties to Iran
Trump has previously described Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as "neutral" during the Iran war.
Moscow and Beijing maintain close ties with Tehran. Russia has said the Iran war could lead to a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Beijing has condemned Washington's attacks on Tehran as a brazen violation of Iran's sovereignty.
Last month, Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran when the Chinese leader visited Washington, and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said at the time.

articles.title: Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iraq faces six-month air defence gap after US-led coalition exit
Iraq faces a potential six-month gap in its air defences following the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces, with new systems not expected to arrive until early next year.
The coalition completed its military withdrawal at the end of September, removing air defence systems that had helped protect parts of the country, including the Kurdistan Region.
Baghdad says agreements have been reached to purchase new equipment, but the first systems could take up to six months to arrive.
The transition has taken on added urgency after two drones targeted a camp for Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
Sabah al-Numan, spokesman for the commander-in-chief of Iraq's armed forces, said Baghdad had made "tangible progress" in acquiring new air defence systems.
He said the first batch would arrive within six months and be deployed across the country.
The package would include advanced radar systems, interceptor weapons and aircraft, he said, as part of a wider plan to strengthen Iraq's control over its airspace.
Numan said the country's security situation remained relatively stable and that Iraqi forces were maintaining a high level of readiness.
However, the announcement leaves questions over Iraq's ability to detect and intercept aerial threats before the new systems become operational.
Iraq has long struggled with limited and ageing air defence capabilities, while drones and missiles have become an increasingly prominent security threat.
A Defence Ministry official nevertheless played down the prospect of an immediate security vacuum.
"The available Iraqi air capabilities are not at a high level, and there is no denying that, but the security situation in the country is relatively calm," the official told The New Arab on condition of anonymity.
The official said Iraq retained "reasonably good capabilities" and that there were currently no expectations of major security breaches.
Concerns are particularly acute in the Kurdistan Region.
Kurdistan Region President Nechirvan Barzani said on Monday that both federal Iraq and the autonomous region required effective air defence coverage.
"Let us be realistic. The Kurdistan Region and Iraq as a whole need an air defence system," he told the MERI Forum in Erbil.
Barzani said an earlier agreement negotiated under former prime minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani with the United States had included plans to provide air defence capabilities covering Kurdistan.
"Air defence is not only a need for the Iraqi state. The Kurdistan Region also needs it," he said.
He also stressed that weapons should remain under state control.
Military expert Aqil al-Shammari warned that the process could take longer than the six months announced by the government.
He said another three months could be required to integrate the equipment, establish command-and-control systems, train personnel, arrange maintenance and complete deployment.
"Owning the system does not mean providing complete air coverage," the former brigadier general told The New Arab.
Shammari said the transition period would be a major test of Baghdad's ability to protect Iraqi airspace.
Kurdish officials had warned before the coalition withdrawal that removing foreign forces and their air defence systems without an immediate replacement could leave the region vulnerable.
The withdrawal forms part of a wider transition towards a new security relationship between Baghdad and Washington focused on training, technology and military co-operation without a direct US combat presence.
They have argued that protecting Kurdistan's airspace is ultimately the responsibility of the federal government because it forms part of Iraq's national airspace.
Those concerns intensified after two explosive-laden drones targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugees near Erbil last week.
No casualties were reported, but the attack renewed fears that gaps in Iraq's air defences could leave the Kurdistan Region vulnerable to further drone strikes.
The withdrawal has also raised wider questions over whether Baghdad can manage its security without the coalition's military presence.

articles.title: As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
articles.body:
As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
A piece of a drone lies in front of a fire truck that arrived to extinguish the aftermath of a Russian strike on Oct. 12, 2026 in Kyiv, Ukraine. On the evening of October 12, a Russian strike drone hit the courtyard of a residential high-rise building. Two people were killed and 11 others were injured in the explosion. (Dan Bashakov/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The attack came as Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the U.S. to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in turn, publicly said that intelligence sharing with the Americans continued, saying on Oct. 13, "Yes, we continue this cooperation."
Multiple sources told the Kyiv Independent that there was no decision to cut intelligence sharing. The incident instead appears to have involved a failure to detect or communicate the missile launch in time to warn Kyiv.
The S-400 is a Russian air defense system with secondary ground-attack capabilities. Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly used the system, as well as its older version, the S-300, to strike Ukrainian cities.
One senior Ukrainian official familiar with the matter said Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said.
"The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The official alleged that the incident might have been "a game" to test Ukraine's reaction. Ukraine's military leadership also warned senior officials that if similar incidents became a pattern, they could indicate that Washington was using intelligence assistance to pressure Kyiv.
There is, however, no evidence in the information provided that the incident resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
Detection of ballistic missile launches is largely carried out by a network of sophisticated infrared detecting spy satellites, which identify the thermal spikes caused by the launch of ballistic missiles, Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The system is generally extremely reliable but not infallible, Hoffmann said, explaining that certain environmental conditions, such as dense, unusually high cloud coverage, could impair its functioning.
Like any system, Hoffmann said, it was susceptible to "human or technical failure" or "extraordinary circumstances" that could impair its functioning.
Missile attacks on Kyiv, which precede air raid warnings, are uncommon but have occurred several times since 2022. In almost all cases, it was the ballistic missiles, which fly at extremely high speeds, that escaped detection by radar.
"Friends, this is not the first time that the intelligence services of our partners have not recorded the launch of the S-400," Zelensky's advisor, Sergey Beskrestnov, said on Oct. 12. "You should not draw conclusions prematurely."

articles.title: US Intelligence Still Flows to Ukraine, Sybiha Says
articles.body:
Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the US, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday, Oct. 13, following concerns that Washington may have suspended the cooperation.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Sybiha was asked about the absence of an advance air raid warning before Russia’s overnight ballistic missile attack.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“You are probably asking me if we are receiving intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation,” Sybiha said, according to The Guardian.
Sybiha did not disclose what types of intelligence Washington continues to provide or whether the scope of the cooperation has changed.
Why Kyiv’s air raid alert was delayed
Sybiha confirmed that the air raid alert during Monday night’s Russian attack was activated late but said this was caused by the weapons Moscow used rather than an interruption in US intelligence sharing.
“It is also true that yesterday’s attack, or nighttime attack, the red alert was launched with a delay, but this was because of the special type of weaponry used by the Russian side,” he said.
Ukraine’s Air Force said it had not received prior information about the launches. The ballistic missiles were detected only after the attack was already underway.
Russia targeted Kyiv with approximately six ballistic missiles at around 10:10 p.m. on Monday, striking transport and warehouse facilities in several districts.
The attack came after a Russian drone struck a residential high-rise earlier in the day. Russian missile and drone attacks across Ukraine from Monday into Tuesday killed two women and injured nine people in Kyiv.
Europe Pushes Back Against Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal, Vows to Keep Sanctions
Ballistic missiles travel at extremely high speeds and follow trajectories that significantly reduce the time available to detect them, activate alerts, and reach shelter.
Reports of US pressure fuel concerns
Questions over intelligence sharing emerged after reports that US officials had threatened to restrict military support unless Ukraine stopped striking Russian oil refineries.
During talks in Miami, US presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly warned Ukrainian negotiators that Washington could suspend intelligence sharing if Kyiv continued its long-range attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure.
A person familiar with the discussions also told Reuters that the US had raised the possibility of restricting weapons procurement through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).
The reported threat followed US President Donald Trump’s calls for Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian refineries amid rising global diesel prices.
An assessment of the possible suspension found that losing US intelligence would particularly affect Ukraine’s early warning against ballistic missiles, although European intelligence and Ukraine’s own surveillance capabilities could replace part of the lost coverage.
Sybiha’s statement indicates that the reported restrictions have not been implemented.
From “no cards” to “don’t play your cards”
Sybiha also argued that Ukraine’s position in relations with its partners had strengthened significantly during the war.
“In less than two years, we have gone from a situation where you have no cards in your hands to a stage where we are told not to play our cards,” he said at the Warsaw Security Forum, according to Ukrinform.
“This is our real achievement and an important lesson that we have learned,” Sybiha added.
He said Ukraine was defending the idea of freedom on the battlefield and paying a high price for it.
According to the foreign minister, the future of Europe, the global security architecture, and the fate of international law are now being decided in Ukraine.
“Ukraine’s front line is Europe’s first line of defense,” he said.

Summarizing the consequences of yet another Russian strike, the President recalled that from the evening until now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different types of weapons: jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles. A significant portion of these weapons was successfully intercepted. But, as Zelenskyy noted, unfortunately, not all of them.
He noted that an ordinary residential building in Kharkiv was destroyed, and the rescue operation lasted virtually all night. Four people were killed in this strike on the building. The President noted that in a single evening, and in Kharkiv alone, 41 people were wounded.
As reported, according to the Ukrainian Air Force, starting at 6:00 p.m. on Monday, October 12, the enemy attacked Ukraine with five “Iskander-M”/S-400 ballistic missiles from the Bryansk region, nine “Banderole”/“Dan-T” loitering munitions, and 108 Shahed-type strike UAVs (74 of which were jet-powered), “Gerbera,” and “Parody”-type decoy drones from the following directions: Orel, Kursk, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russian Federation), the temporarily occupied city of Donetsk, and Hvardeiske (temporarily occupied Crimea).
According to preliminary data, as of 8:00 a.m. on Tuesday, October 13, air defense forces shot down or neutralized 88 drones. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, and downed targets (debris) were found at seven locations.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Fighter Fleet Has Quietly Tipped West—F-16s and Mirages Now Outnumber Soviet Jets
articles.body:
- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine’s Fighter Fleet Has Quietly Tipped West—F-16s and Mirages Now Outnumber Soviet Jets
Ukraine’s Air Force is no longer primarily a Soviet-designed fleet—the combined number of F-16s and Mirage 2000s has now overtaken its remaining MiG-29s and Su-27s, with Gripens and Rafales potentially next.
Ukraine’s air defense against Russia’s increasingly common jet-powered Shahed-type drones relies on far more than ground-based interceptors, with fighter aviation becoming an increasingly important part of the layered defense. According to Defense Express on October 13, the balance inside Ukraine’s combat aviation fleet has now shifted significantly toward Western aircraft.
Ukraine is using both F-16s and French Mirage 2000s to intercept fast-moving Russian drones, while work is underway to stock enough ammunition for several months of sustained operations and eliminate maintenance bottlenecks that limit how many aircraft can remain mission-ready at any given time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Those priorities were recently outlined following discussions between Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara and journalists.
The key change, Defense Express notes, is numerical. Although MiG-29s and Su-27s still remain important to Ukrainian combat aviation, the combined fleet of Western F-16s and Mirage 2000s now exceeds the number of those two Soviet-designed fighter types still in service.
MiG-29s and Su-27s are still very much in the fight
That shift does not mean Ukraine’s Soviet-era fighters have disappeared from air-defense operations. Defense Express points to regularly published footage showing Ukrainian MiG-29s intercepting Russian jet-powered UAVs, making clear that those aircraft continue to perform combat missions alongside Western fighters.
MiG-29s and Su-27s remain useful because Ukrainian pilots and maintenance crews have decades of experience operating them, while the aircraft can still perform both interception and strike missions.
Their long-term challenge is sustainability: battlefield losses, shrinking stocks of compatible weapons, and increasingly difficult access to spare parts make it harder to maintain the fleets at their former scale.
This also explains why official discussions about fighter aviation increasingly center on F-16s and Mirage 2000s. They are not the only aircraft being used, but they are becoming the dominant part of Ukraine’s available fighter force and increasingly shape how the Air Force plans future operations.
Jet-powered Shaheds are driving fighter demand
The role of fighter aircraft has become more important as Russia introduces faster jet-powered UAVs, which give mobile ground teams less time to detect and engage incoming targets.
Fighters can patrol much larger areas, rapidly reposition as drone routes shift, and provide another interception layer between inexpensive drone-defense systems and scarce long-range surface-to-air missiles.
Ukraine is therefore working not only to increase the number of Western aircraft available but also to ensure they have sufficient ammunition and can be serviced quickly enough to sustain a high operational tempo.
According to Defense Express, one of the priorities is building missile and ammunition stocks several months ahead while addressing maintenance bottlenecks that can leave otherwise available aircraft grounded.
In September 2026 alone, Ukrainian combat aircraft reportedly conducted about 1,300 sorties for fighter cover and more than 250 missions against ground targets.
There is no public breakdown by aircraft type, but Defense Express argues that the growing numerical share of F-16s and Mirage 2000s makes it likely that Western fighters accounted for a significant portion of that activity.
Gripen and Rafale could push the transition even further
The move away from a primarily Soviet-designed fighter fleet may accelerate further. Ukraine is already looking toward Sweden’s JAS 39 Gripen and France’s Rafale as potential future additions, a transition also highlighted by the Royal United Services Institute in an August 2026 assessment.
If those aircraft eventually enter Ukrainian service, the Air Force’s center of gravity would shift even more decisively toward Western platforms, logistics, weapons, and maintenance systems.
MiG-29s and Su-27s would still remain useful for as long as they can be sustained, but they would increasingly operate alongside a fleet built around entirely different standards.
The result is an Air Force already well into a structural transition: Soviet fighters remain active and relevant, but F-16s and Mirage 2000s now hold the numerical advantage—and the next generation of Ukrainian combat aviation may be even more Western.
Previously, Ukraine’s air defense forces reported the destruction of more than 445,000 Russian missiles, attack drones, reconnaissance aircraft, and other aerial targets since the start of the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

articles.title: North Korea unveils copy of Canadian armored vehicle
articles.body:
- Kim Jong Un opened a new underground-style defense museum displaying the Hwasong-20 ICBM, new missiles and drones.
- Among the exhibits is a new 4x4 armored vehicle closely resembling the Canadian Roshel Senator used by Ukraine in Kursk.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has opened a new national defense museum packed with the country’s missiles, rocket launchers and drones, and among the exhibits is a previously unseen 4×4 armored vehicle that closely resembles the Canadian-made Roshel Senator used by Ukraine.
State news agency KCNA reported on Oct. 13 that Kim attended the opening of the Defense Revolution Museum, run by the Second Economy Commission that oversees North Korea’s arms industry, on Oct. 11 and vowed to keep developing the country’s weapons. KCNA quoted him calling the museum a “precious monument” and did not give its size or location, though photos suggest at least part of it was built underground, with weapons lined up in long, tunnel-like halls.
The new armored vehicle shown in KCNA photos shares the overall layout and several hull details of the Senator, a Canadian armored car built on a Ford F-550 truck chassis that Roshel has supplied to Ukraine in large numbers. The North Korean version appears to have a lengthened body, suggesting it has been adapted to carry more troops in the back. KCNA did not name the vehicle or give any details about its protection, engine or how many are in service.
North Korean troops know the Senator from the battlefield. Ukrainian units used Senators during their incursion into Russia’s Kursk region in August 2024, where thousands of North Korean soldiers later fought alongside Russian forces to push Ukraine out. Russian troops have captured several Senators intact or lightly damaged, including one taken by naval infantry in the Kursk region that month, and a captured vehicle may have been handed to North Korea, which now appears to be building its own version. Roshel has delivered more than 2,000 Senators to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion, and open-source tracking project Oryx had documented 182 in Mrap version and 83 Senator IMV of them destroyed, damaged or captured by the end of 2025.
The museum’s largest exhibit is the Hwasong-20 intercontinental ballistic missile, which North Korea has displayed but not yet flight-tested, shown with a world map suggesting it could reach the United States and beyond. Visitors also see a new submarine-launched ballistic missile, the 600 mm super-large multiple rocket launcher and a range of drones developed under Kim’s rule.
Kim opened the museum a day after North Korea test-fired what KCNA described as a tactical ballistic missile, which state media said brought “an important change” in improving all of the country’s weapons systems. Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi condemned the launch. The museum opening also came as U.S. President Donald Trump said he might meet Kim during a planned trip to Asia in mid-November.

articles.title: EU Blacklists Nearly 1,600 in Russian Defense Firms and Executives
articles.body:
The European Union adopted its largest-ever single set of sanctions against Russia to date on Monday, blacklisting 1,569 individuals and companies within the country's military-industrial complex.
The measures blacklist 826 Russian companies and 743 chief executives, bringing the total number of listings under the EU sanctions regime protecting Ukraine’s territorial integrity to nearly 4,600. The designated entities face immediate asset freezes and funding blocks, while the targeted individuals are now barred from entering the bloc.
The package specifically targets mid-level suppliers that form the "core" of Russia's defense sector, which together generate an annual turnover of at least 20 billion euros ($22.32 billion) and employ more than 250,000 people.
According to the European Council, the designated companies supply critical components for advanced weapons systems, including semiconductors, radars, satellite systems, explosives, and optics. Notably, more than half of the new listings address the production chain for the ballistic missiles Russia uses in its daily strikes against Ukrainian infrastructure.
"Bombing Kyiv’s bridges, ships transporting grain, and the National Academy of Sciences are not the actions of a country seeking peace," said Kaja Kallas, the EU's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The sweeping European measures come just three days after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an agreement on Truth Social with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets in an effort to lower domestic fuel costs.
Further commenting on the latest EU sanctions, Kallas, however, stressed: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Moscow but to increase it."
The new listings follow the European Council's June 2026 directive to intensify pressure on Moscow in response to an escalating military campaign that has deliberately targeted civilian infrastructure and, according to the Council, aims to undermineUkraine's resilience.

Kiev loses 1,285 troops along engagement line in past day - latest figures

articles.title: North Korean missile launches may be response to South's hypersonic test, Seoul says
articles.body:
North Korea's launch of multiple ballistic missiles towards the East Sea appears to be an apparent response to South Korea's successful test of a hypersonic glide vehicle last week, the South Korean military has confirmed.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected the launches originating from the Pyongyang region.
At least one projectile flew more than 900 kilometres, Yonhap News Agency said.
JCS spokesperson Jang Do-young said the firing could also demonstrate technical advances under Pyongyang's five-year defence modernisation blueprint.
Jang declined to confirm whether the weapons tested were hypersonic systems or intermediate-range ballistic missiles, noting that further technical analysis is ongoing.
The launches followed South Korea’s inaugural test of a hypersonic glide vehicle on Thursday.
Regional reactions
Japan's defence authorities confirmed detecting two suspected ballistic missiles, reporting that the projectiles landed in waters outside its exclusive economic zone.
The US Pacific Command issued a statement confirming close consultations with regional allies: "Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies."
The command reiterated Washington's ironclad commitment to defending regional partners.
The missile tests unfold amid friction along the inter-Korean border following a September 21 landmine detonation inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) that injured three South Korean soldiers, two critically.
Seoul accused North Korean forces of deliberately laying the explosives following a joint inquiry with the UN Command.
Pyongyang rejected the findings as fabricated and warned it would retaliate against any countermeasures.
Pyongyang has not issued an official public statement regarding Monday's launches.

France Explores Nuclear Microreactors to Power Military Bases and Field Operations
France’s army is considering the use of compact nuclear reactors to supply electricity to military installations, command centers, and field hospitals as part of a broader effort to modernize its battlefield energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the French Army’s Déclinaison capacitaire d’Action Aéroterrestre Future (DCF) document, published by its Future Combat Command (CCF), nuclear microreactors are among several technologies being examined to improve energy independence and operational capabilities.
The official document identifies energy production and storage as priorities for future ground operations, with containerized nuclear reactors emerging as one potential solution for supplying electricity to military facilities.
These compact installations could provide power to command posts, logistics centers, and deployed medical facilities, potentially reducing dependence on conventional fuel deliveries and external electricity networks. French military planners have identified three areas of energy development.
The first focuses on compact, high-energy-density batteries for individual soldiers and robotic systems, intended to increase available power without significantly increasing equipment weight.
The second involves hybrid propulsion and the electrification of armored vehicles. These technologies could reduce vehicle detectability while supplying additional electricity to onboard systems.
The third focuses on evaluating containerized nuclear reactors as an alternative source of electricity for military operations.
However, France has not announced a procurement program or selected a manufacturer. It remains unclear whether the army would adapt existing commercial reactor technology or pursue a system developed specifically for military applications.
The proposal remains at the research and capability-planning stage, with no confirmed deployment timeline.
Separately, France has been expanding its nuclear defense capabilities. On March 2, President Emmanuel Macron announced plans to increase the country’s nuclear warhead stockpile and stop publicly disclosing its size, citing a deteriorating global security environment.
He also confirmed that France’s next-generation nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine, Invincible, is scheduled to enter service in 2036.

Trump said he does not believe Russia and China are helping Iran
Kyiv • UNN

articles.title: Critics warn of espionage risks, loss of trust within NATO as Slovakia restores military-diplomatic representation with Russia
articles.body:
Concern as Slovakia restores military contacts with Russia
October 13, 2026
When Robert Fico sat opposite Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin in May, the Slovak prime minister said relations between their countries should extend beyond energy supplies.
He told the Russian president that steps had already been taken to restore military attaches at their respective embassies.
Five months later, the arrangement is now taking shape.
Slovakia has sent two military officers — Brigadier General Slavomir Staviarsky and his deputy, Colonel Ivo Gahir — to Moscow and is preparing to receive a Russian military attache in Bratislava, restoring military-diplomatic representation for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
What has Slovakia to gain?
The move has prompted criticism from opposition politicians, who question what Slovakia stands to gain.
They warn that Russia could use the arrangement to strengthen its intelligence operations.
"One additional military attache does not fundamentally change that broader picture; the appointment's main significance is the political signal it sends," Martin Poliacik, a former Slovak MP affiliated with the opposition Progressive Slovakia party, told DW.
"NATO allies should be concerned both about the activities of the incoming officer and about the political environment in which he will operate," he went on.
The appointments were reported by Slovak news website Aktuality.sk on October 8. Both officers appear on the Slovak Defense Ministry's published list of military diplomats serving abroad.
According to public broadcaster STVR, Staviarsky has been in Moscow since the beginning of August.
Meanwhile, opposition defense experts quoted by Aktuality.sk named the incoming Russian officer as Maxim Verezan.
Verezan has received Slovak approval, according to the opposition sources cited by the website, but was not yet listed among accredited military attaches.
Aktuality.sk says that the Defense Ministry has not answered its question as to when Verezan is due to arrive in Bratislava.
Fear of espionage and disinformation
The prospect has revived memories of a Russian espionage scandal involving Sergei Solomasov, the Russian embassy's deputy military attache in Bratislava, a few years ago.
Solomasov was filmed recruiting and handing over money to Bohus Garbar, a contributor to the pro-Russian website Hlavne spravy, in 2021.
Solomasov was expelled from Slovakia the following year. Garbar was subsequently convicted of espionage and bribery.
Opposition experts told Aktuality.sk that a Slovak attache in Moscow would be closely watched and obtain little useful information, while the reciprocal Russian posting could facilitate espionage in Slovakia.
They warned that the incoming officer could conduct influence and disinformation operations, questioning what Slovakia would receive in return.
Government defends the move
The Slovak government and its supporters have defended the renewal of contacts as a means of gathering information and maintaining diplomatic representation.
In a statement reported by Slovak public broadcaster STVR, Slovak military intelligence said Staviarsky's role was to assess the security and military-political situation and keep the Defense Ministry informed.
Richard Gluck, a member of Fico's Smer party who chairs parliament's defense and security committee, pointed to the presence of American, British and French military diplomats in Moscow.
"We were losing a great deal of information," Gluck told STVR, arguing that ending Slovakia's military diplomatic presence in Moscow had been a mistake.
'A very serious step'
For retired Lieutenant General Pavel Macko, however, the circumstances in which the previous contacts ended are crucial.
"This is a very serious step taken by the Fico government," said Macko, a former Slovak deputy chief of defense and once the highest-ranking Slovak general in NATO's command structures.
"Nothing has changed [since 2022], just the opposite," he went on.
"Russia's adversarial activities continue to grow in Slovakia and in the region. The Russian war of aggression against Ukraine continues with high intensity, so do the hostile hybrid activities against Slovakia and its neighbors," Macko said.
He pointed to a foiled plot to burn down a Ukrainian-owned drone factory in eastern Slovakia and suspicions that incidents in Munich and Leipzig were linked to Russian operations based in Slovakia.
Macko also warned that political influence over Slovakia's intelligence services and the government's pro-Russian policies could further damage intelligence-sharing and trust among allies, despite the presence of "a significant number of very professional and trustworthy officers."
One eye on next year's election?
Martin Poliacik, meanwhile, said he suspected political motives lay behind the decision to restore the military attache posts, which comes as Prime Minister Fico eyes his chances of re-election next year.
"[Fico's] best chance of building a credible narrative for the next election is to claim that everyone else is dragging us into war and he alone wants peace," Poliacik told DW.
"I believe he will argue that he is best placed to talk to Putin about ending the war, and that this requires an exceptionally close relationship with him," he went on, adding that Fico tried to keep quiet about the major role played by Slovak arms manufacturers in supplying Ukraine with ammunition.
The ammunition is supplied under commercial contracts, rather than as military aid from the Slovak government.
Poliacik, too, distinguished between Slovakia's formal commitments and confidence in its political leadership. In his view, Western partners have become accustomed to Fico's behavior.
"Slovakia is formally fulfilling its NATO commitments," he went on.
"Formal compliance does not, by itself, settle the question of political trust," Poliacik added. "Predictability, however, is not the same as reliability."
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

articles.title: The night Trump announced a diesel deal with Putin, drones knocked out more than half the tanks at a Russian fuel-export terminal
articles.body:
A drone strike on 10 October put more than half of the large fuel tanks out of action at an oil-loading terminal in Russia’s Rostov-on-Don, Russian news Telegram channel Astra found. The terminal loads fuel onto river and sea tankers for export, and it burned for two days while a local channel wrote that reeds might be on fire. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has officially acknowledged the hit. It came hours after US President Donald Trump announced a diesel deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Russia has spent the autumn hammering Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter. Ukraine’s long-range drones keep hitting the refineries, depots, and terminals that fuel Russia’s army and earn it export revenue. Every burned tank turns that revenue into repair bills, while Moscow is already subsidizing its own fuel pumps. A refinery-only truce of the kind the White House described a day after the strike would shield the Russian plants that feed terminals like this one.
Seven of 12 tanks out of action
Astra’s analysts concluded from eyewitness footage that at least seven of the terminal’s 12 large tanks had been knocked out. Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ counted seven burned-out tanks and one more scorched by the fire.
The fire was still burning in the early hours of 12 October. Local channel Rostov Glavny posted video of the burning tank farm, passing on rumors that reeds were on fire and noting the city’s second day under smoke, The Moscow Times reported. Footage filmed in the daytime on 12 October showed no more open flames, only gray smoke, according to Astra.
A terminal that loads fuel for export
The site is the oil-loading terminal of the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Products Plant, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny District. It receives, stores, and transships fuel onto river and sea tankers, including for export, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said.
The terminal also supplies fuel to the Russian army and earns Moscow hard currency, ZN reported. The Moscow Times put its loading capacity at 3.5 million tons a year and its tank farm at about 60,000 cubic meters, roughly 16 million gallons.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
The refinery itself stands in the town of Novoshakhtinsk near the border with Russian-occupied Luhansk Oblast. The terminal sits on the Don River with access to the Sea of Azov, Ukrainian military outlet Militarnyi noted. Ukraine hit the refinery in June, and Ukraine’s General Staff reported striking the Yug Rusi terminal on 9 July, placing it in Bataysk.
A night of drones over the region
Exilenova+ posted images of the burning terminal in the early hours of 10 October. It presented them as the site after Trump’s phone call with Putin. The channel later shared NASA satellite fire data showing the blaze.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yuri Slyusar claimed the attack injured six people. Slyusar further stated air defenses downed more than 100 drones over the region. Radio Liberty’s Russian Service noted that neither side had officially confirmed the hit on the terminal.
Hours after the US-Russia diesel deal
The strike came hours after Trump announced on 9 October that Russia had agreed to supply diesel to US and global markets. The US Treasury then cleared the trade with a sanctions license.
On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. Under it, he expects Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, a White House official told Axios.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that evening that Ukraine’s armed forces had received all relevant orders. Neither Ukrainian monitoring channels nor Russian officials have reported a new strike on a Russian oil facility since. On 13 October, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to guarantee an energy ceasefire if Russia took matching steps.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: No warning from partners about Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv
articles.body:
Zelenskyy: No warning from partners about Russian ballistic strike on Kyiv
Commenting on Russia's recent attacks on Ukrainian cities, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine received no warning from its partners about the ballistic missile strike on Kyiv on the evening of 12 October.
Source: Zelenskyy on X (Twitter), as reported by European Pravda
Details: Zelenskyy noted that starting that evening and continuing into 13 October, Russia attacked Ukraine with more than 100 different weapons, including jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles. A significant proportion were shot down, but not all of them.
"There was also a particularly vile ballistic missile strike on Kyiv – five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, we received no early warning from our partners about this strike," Zelenskyy said.
He stressed that intelligence about Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives and is one of the most critical issues.
"This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," the president added.
Zelenskyy also said that Ukraine has not struck Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for two days since US President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire.
"During this time, the Russians have attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure, sending absolutely clear signals that they have no intention of refraining from strikes on Ukraine. [...] Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal steps toward de-escalation, and effective pressure on Russia is needed to make de-escalation happen. Wars end when the aggressor realises that it cannot prolong the war," Zelenskyy stressed.
He added that international pressure on Russia contributes to bringing peace closer.
"But direct or indirect support for Russia, slowing down assistance to Ukraine, and making it harder to protect lives against ballistic missiles will certainly not help bring peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed," Zelenskyy concluded.
Background:
- Earlier, it was reported that during talks with the Ukrainian team in Florida on Friday 9 October, Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine because of Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
- Reuters sources denied that any such threats had been made.
- Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, meanwhile, has said that Ukraine continues to receive intelligence from the United States.

articles.title: Putin wants Ukraine deal more than Zelensky – Trump
articles.body:
Putin wants Ukraine deal more than Zelensky – Trump
Russian President Vladimir Putin is more eager than Vladimir Zelensky to reach a deal to end the Ukraine conflict, US President Donald Trump has said. Trump’s comments came after he suggested it is time for Ukraine to get a “new president.”
Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump claimed both Moscow and Kiev support the energy ceasefire which he announced on Sunday. Neither Russia nor Ukraine has confirmed the truce.
“I think they want to make a deal, but they don’t know how. But we’re going to get them to make a deal,” Trump said.
“I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky,” he added.
Trump also rejected criticism of his decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel following a phone call with Putin on Friday, stressing that the agreement benefited the wider world and American farmers and ranchers. 
“Zelensky has to focus on making a deal, not talking about that,” he stressed, referring to the Ukrainian leader’s criticism of the agreement.
On Sunday, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire.” Zelensky said the announcement “was news for me,” but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has declined to confirm the agreement, saying contacts were ongoing. While praising the efforts of American negotiators, Peskov stressed that Moscow is seeking long-term peace rather than a temporary ceasefire. Russian officials have long argued that a truce would only help Ukraine to reinforce its battered military and receive more Western-made weapons.
According to the New York Times, Ukrainian officials were informed of the US-Russia diesel deal during tense negotiations in Miami. The US delegation subsequently demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries, and when Kiev’s representatives asked what they would receive in return, the Americans reportedly argued that Washington already provided substantial assistance, including intelligence sharing. Some participants interpreted this as a veiled threat to withdraw support, the article said.
Following his conversation with Putin and Zelensky’s angry reaction to the diesel deal, Trump suggested that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.” Zelensky’s presidential term expired more than two years ago, although the Ukrainian leader has refused to hold a new election, citing martial law. Russia has declared Zelensky “illegitimate,” highlighting his dubious legal status as a major obstacle to a peace agreement.
After a war of words with Trump, Zelensky signaled he was ready to hold an election but demanded a 60-day ceasefire with Russia. Moscow responded by stressing that “if Kiev genuinely wants to hold elections… then the president of the Russian Federation… will be ready to issue an order not to carry out strikes against Ukraine on the election day specifically.”

articles.title: Fact check: Russia turns to AI to push fakes about 'women's draft' in Ukraine
articles.body:
Fact check: Russia turns to AI to push fakes about 'women's draft' in Ukraine
Servicewomen of the “Fighting Witches” mobile group of Ukraine’s Air Defense Forces practice shooting at a base in Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Nov. 2, 2024. (Yevhenii Vasyliev/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Russian disinformation yet again targets the sensitive topic of mobilization in Ukraine — this time, pushing falsehoods about an alleged forced draft of women.
Pro-Kremlin social media accounts and Russian media have spread AI-generated images alleging that Ukrainian women are being lured to join the Armed Forces by targeted recruitment posters, while others claim they are being outright called up for military service.
But though tens of thousands of Ukrainian women enlisted in the army as volunteers, these claims are false — there is no mandatory draft of women in place, nor is it being prepared.
Telegram channels have once again proven to be fertile ground for such fabricated stories, with both Ukrainian- and Russian-language channels involved in spreading them.
One fake post from Sept. 15 alleged that posters featuring women in military uniforms had appeared around Odesa, a city in southern Ukraine. Other channels reposted identical photographs but claimed they had been seen around Lutsk, in western Ukraine.
The banners' message was intended to show how domestic chores hardly differ from tasks at the front, reading, "You figured out the washing machine — you'll figure out FPVs (first-person-view drones) too."
"There were no such banners, and an AI verification tool indicates they were AI-generated," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, told the Kyiv Independent.
LetsData spotted the campaign in mid-September as it began circulating on social media.
A similar fake image was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian state TV presenter Olesya Loseva on Sept. 29. The post featured a bogus advertisement she claimed had been displayed in one of Kyiv's shopping centers.
The image features a young woman standing over a baby and a gun, with the Ukrainian-language caption reading: "A real Ukrainian woman can do these things in 40 seconds!"
When the Kyiv Independent ran this image through Hive Moderation, a platform that detects AI-generated or synthetic content, it returned a near-certain verdict — 99.9% likely to be AI-generated.
"This narrative is recurring and gets amplified from time to time, meaning that it comes and goes, sometimes using 'new tools' like AI-generated imagery," adds Osadchuk.
While disinformation and propaganda have long been central to Moscow's arsenal, Russia is now harnessing AI to spread falsehoods faster and more widely.
"Russia-linked actors have mostly used AI tools to amplify existing tactics, such as producing inauthentic content at scale and spreading content to reach broader audiences and fuel polarization," the European Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats reported in March.
read also
Besides Telegram, the narrative has also appeared on X, where a post by Donbass Segodnya, a pro-Russian news outlet, featured images of a woman apparently holding summons papers, implying that a mass call-up of women has begun.
Women can indeed receive summonses, but only if they are in the military register, which is mandatory only for women with relevant medical or pharmaceutical education.
Even then, this does not mean they can be mobilized against their will. The women are simply added to the register and can be summoned to update their personal data or undergo a medical examination.
No mobilization of women in Ukraine
Since 2022, Ukraine has been carrying out a large-scale draft of military-age men to boost its army's ranks and resist Russian aggression — a topic repeatedly targeted by Russian disinformation and propaganda.
Women have also joined the military as volunteers, with about 76,000 being part of Ukraine's Armed Forces, including 57,000 serving in military roles. However, Ukraine has not instituted a mandatory draft for women.
"There are no decisions to mobilize women in Ukraine," said Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, a body at the country's National Security and Defense Council, on Aug. 26.
"The parliamentary committee on national security, defense, and intelligence officially stated that there are no legislative initiatives, draft laws, or internal discussions concerning the introduction of such mobilization.
Moscow launched this latest disinformation campaign just as rumors of women's conscription circulated in Ukraine.
Former Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov raised the issue in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) on Aug. 20, arguing that requiring women to serve in the military would "immediately double the mobilization pool."
Separately, former U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg said on Aug. 24 that he believed women should be mobilized to help Ukraine's manpower problem since "they (women) fight no worse than men."
The Ukrainian parliament reacted by saying that the comments "do not reflect the actual legislative work."
With no draft law on the table, the mobilization of women remains confined to AI-generated content.

articles.title: The partners did not warn Ukraine about the launch of ballistic missiles at Kyiv on Monday — Zelenskyy
articles.body:
The partners did not warn Ukraine about the launch of ballistic missiles at Kyiv on Monday — Zelenskyy
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that the partners did not warn Ukraine about the launch of five ballistic missiles at Kyiv. Four people were killed in Kharkiv.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that partners did not warn Ukraine about the launch of ballistic missiles at Kyiv on Monday, October 12. Zelenskyy wrote about this on Telegram, reports UNN.
Details
"From the evening until now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different means of attack: jet-powered drones, loitering munitions, and ballistic missiles. A significant portion of these attack weapons was shot down. But, unfortunately, not all of them. In Kharkiv, an ordinary residential building was destroyed, and the rescue operation lasted practically the entire night — people were being searched for under the rubble. Four people were killed in this strike on the building in Kharkiv. My condolences to all the relatives and loved ones. A total of 41 people were wounded in just one evening and only in Kharkiv," Zelenskyy wrote.
He noted that there had also been a rather treacherous ballistic strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure.
"Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence data about the launch of Russian ballistic missiles helps save people's lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles," Zelenskyy added.
The President emphasized that Ukraine had not carried out strikes against Russian oil refining facilities or the energy sector in general for two days from the moment the US president announced a ceasefire in the energy sector, but Russia did not heed Trump.
"During this time, the Russians attacked both our energy facilities and our critical infrastructure and sent absolutely clear signals that they were not going to refrain from strikes against Ukraine. Over these two days, 19 regions of our country came under attack. Our position remains unchanged: Ukraine is ready for reciprocal de-escalatory steps, and effective pressure on Russia is needed for de-escalation to take place. Wars end when the aggressor feels that it has no ability to prolong the war. The world's pressure on Russia contributes precisely to this — bringing peace closer. But direct or indirect support for Russia, delaying assistance to Ukraine, and complicating the protection of lives from ballistic missiles are things that will definitely not contribute to peace. Everyone needs peace. A strong America, a strong Europe, and strong partners are needed," the President concluded.
We remind you
On the evening of October 12, several explosions were heard in Kyiv, but the air-raid alert sounded only after the attack. At 22:09, the Air Force reported a "high-speed target heading toward Kyiv".
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the President of Ukraine, questioned the assumption that the strike on Kyiv, which took place without an "air raid alert" being announced, occurred because the United States had allegedly stopped transmitting intelligence to Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine’s largest steelworks begins cold shutdown after extensive damage from Russian strikes, saying safe operation is impossible while war continues
articles.body:
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih has begun the process of placing its plant in cold shutdown following four Russian missile attacks, the company said on 10 October. The attacks killed six workers, injured more than 18 others, and forced the suspension of primary steel production.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih is Ukraine’s largest steelworks, so its shutdown adds to the pressure on an industry already hit by Russian attacks and disrupted exports.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih CEO Mauro Longobardo said the company’s priority was to protect workers and industrial assets. He said the ArcelorMittal Group would remain in Ukraine, but that its assessment was that safe operation was impossible while the war continued.
Workers and the city
As of July, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and its subsidiaries employed about 17,000 people, local outlet Pershyi Kryvorizkyi reported. On 29 September, the outlet reported that the company had not said how many workers could lose their jobs and was assessing its staffing needs after production stopped. It also said municipal water and heating utilities had about 1,000 vacancies and had been instructed to help ArcelorMittal workers find jobs. The outlet noted that it was unclear whether the vacancies were new and that the announcement did not specify the roles or salaries.
In late September, Kryvyi Rih defense council head Oleksandr Vilkul wrote on Telegram that the city would cut spending and stop a number of projects as tax revenues fell. He attributed the pressure to Russian attacks and the inability to export through seaports, and said several major industrial facilities were idle, including ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih and three mining and ore-processing plants.
September steel output down 4.7-fold
Ukraine’s steel production fell 4.7-fold year on year in September, to 131,000 tons, the steelmakers’ association Ukrmetalurhprom said, NV reported. Metinvest chief operating officer Oleksandr Myronenko told Forbes Ukraine on 15 September that the group would declare force majeure on some contracts after Zaporizhstal and Kametstal halted operations.
An expected $1 billion impairment
The ArcelorMittal Group said on 25 September that it expected to record a non-cash impairment of about $1 billion, mostly related to property, plant, and equipment. It also said it had provided more than $700 million in financial support to its Ukrainian business.
