articles.title: MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
articles.body:
MI5 chief warns of threats to UK from Russia, Iran and AI
- Published
MI5 is devoting more resource to countering state threats than during the Cold War, the head of the intelligence service has said.
Sir Ken McCallum said threats from foreign adversaries had quadrupled in the last decade, with Russia "aggressor number one" as well as increased Iran-linked aggression against Jewish sites and military bases.
At an annual speech in London, MI5's chief said Russia was waging hybrid warfare at a time when AI was "supercharging the cyber-security contest between attackers and defenders".
He also warned of rising threats from "extreme right-wing terrorism" and said MI5 had "caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al," including by integrating the technology with drones.
He said the biggest threat from the misuse of AI was extremist groups using the technology to harness new and existing bioweapons.
Sir Ken said Russia had stopped short of "conventional conflict" against Nato and is instead trying to unsettle European countries while its progress in its full-scale invasion of Ukraine is "minimal and horrifically costly".
Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyber-attacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.
These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.
Sir Ken said MI5 successes in identifying and expelling Russian spies from the UK had left the Kremlin dependent on paying proxies for attempted attacks.
"With its traditional covert footprint eviscerated by almost 1,000 expulsions since the invasion, the Kremlin's global toolkit is weak, he said.
"So we see them scrambling to pay criminals to do their bidding."
He added: "These are not the actions of a great power with the strategic upper hand."
His comments come as a growing number of leaders across Europe have warned Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine.
Asked after the speech about Prime Minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that Russia interfered with the Brexit referendum, Sir Ken said this was "not new news" and there was a difference between "interference attempted" and "outcome achieved".
He said it was a matter of public record that there were pieces in Russian media and "so-called internet trolls and bot farms" seeking to influence the Brexit debate, but also stressed that the result of the 2016 referendum was "not in dispute".
He added that he was "worried" about the the ongoing debate on Russian interference.
"I am a little bit anxious that we don't play into our adversaries' hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall," he told reporters.
Meanwhile, Sir Ken warned that Iran is also expanding a hybrid campaign in the UK.
The intelligence chief said there had been 50 arrests in the last year over Iran-linked activities.
Much of this Iranian aggression has been aimed at Jewish communities, Sir Ken added, and also at "harder targets, like military sites".
Sir Ken did not mention arrests at RAF Fairford directly during his speech, but told reporters afterwards the incident was "not unique".
He added: "We have seen Iranian interest beyond RAF Fairford in the UK."
The incident at the airbase in Gloucesteshire, where three suspicious vans were seen parked nearby, has seen seven people arrested and bailed by counter-terrorism police.
Burnham has said the incident was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard".
The MI5 head said in his speech: "What I can say is that those who seek to cause mayhem on British streets - whether hired thugs here or their paymasters overseas - will meet an unflinching response."
Sir Ken added that the National Security Act - a 2023 law designed to target people working against UK interests for foreign powers - is in heavy use, and has been employed to tackle threats from China as well as Iran and Russia.
On the emerging threat posed by AI, Sir Ken said: "It can produce propaganda and radicalising material tailored to the individual.
"We've caught terrorists seeking to exploit Al to improve their reconnaissance and attack methodologies, with Al-enabled drones adding a new twist."
Sir Ken said the bioweapons threat posed by AI was "not yet realised" but warned the technology has the "potential to change the stakes".
"These risks are real. The UK Intelligence Community - MI5, GCHQ, MI6 - is working closely with the UK's globally respected AI Security Institute to take them on."
Sir Ken said AI poses unknown threats, telling Thames House: "Put at its simplest, human history has given us no experience of facing an actor which is smarter than we are".
He announced MI5 had launched an AI Threat Assessment Centre, which he said would assess sources and "separate the bluster from the realities".
In April, the UK's terrorism threat level was raised to severe for the first time in five years, meaning an attack is highly likely.
Sir Ken said Islamist groups like Al Qaeda and so-called Islamic State both continue to direct and inspire attacks, while the increased risk was also driven "in significant part" by extreme right-wing terrorism.
He continued: "Over the last year the most marked trend has been an increase in cases where extremist versions of anti-immigration and anti-Muslim grievance are tipping into terrorist intent."
Sir Ken said extreme right-wing terrorism tended to "skew young", driven by the internet - adding that MI5 had in recent months investigated a "radicalised extreme right-wing 13-year-old here in the UK".
He said: "That investigation generated insight that enabled one of our international partners to prevent a lethal attack on their soil."

articles.title: Hezbollah rebuilds military capabilities, upgrades FPV drones ahead of possible Israel war - report
articles.body:
Hezbollah is preparing to rearm and rebuild its terror capabilities in the event of an escalation with the IDF amid rising regional tensions, sources told Beirut-based independent news outlet Al-Modon on Monday.
Al-Modon is managed by the Qatari-based Fadaat Media Group, and often takes a critical stance against the Iran-backed Shi'ite terror group, while calling for a pro-Arab consensus.
"If a large-scale war breaks out, it will reach Lebanon. Israeli is waiting for any opportunity for military escalation against Hezbollah, as it is working to convince Washington of the need to renew the war against Iran. Just as Tehran is anticipating the possibility of war against it, Hezbollah is preparing and equipping itself," the report said.
According to the outlet, the Iranian proxy terror group takes "Israeli threats seriously and is dealing with messages conveyed through diplomatic channels indicating that Israel will not abandon its military escalation and is waiting for the appropriate timing."
Sources told the outlet that Hezbollah is "anticipating" war and "has succeeded in taking advantage of the extended ceasefire period to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon, both south and north of the Litani River."
Lebanese Armed Forces seize truck transporting Hezbollah explosives planned for FPV drone improvements
The sources also linked Hezbollah's rebuilding of militarist terror capabilities to the interception of a truck that was transporting explosive materials from the Bekaa Valley to Beirut.
The Jerusalem Post reported on Sunday that the Lebanese Armed Forces seized a truck at a checkpoint in the Bekaa Valley, which was carrying hundreds of kilograms of explosives belonging to the terror group, including TNT and C4.
Two suspects admitted to receiving the explosives from a Hezbollah commander in Baalbek, with instructions to transport them to Beirut, the Post reported at the time.
Sources told the Lebanese outlet that the terror group uses the materials found in such trucks to develop first-person view (FPV) drones, which have been upgraded to carry between four and six kilograms of explosives, compared with the previous payload of 2.5 kg.
Hezbollah terrorists have also succeeded in extending the length of the FPV's cables from 20km. to over 30km., meaning that the terror group can attack targets from a further distance, the sources said.
The terror group has also continued to work towards reinforcing its capabilities by increasing military deployments in villages and towns adjacent to the Yellow Line, including in some areas south of the Litani River, particularly in the vicinity of Nabatiya, the report noted.
The terror group has also taken security precautions in anticipation of possible Israeli assassination attempts targeting terror leaders and officials, the report said. This included the evacuation of many apartments and offices in Beirut's southern suburbs, including the Hezbollah stronghold of Dahiyeh.
Beirut has not taken enough steps towards disarming Hezbollah terrorists, Israel believes - report
The outlet also highlighted that Israeli believes the Lebanese state has not fulfilled its duty towards the framework agreement surrounding Hezbollah disarmament. In this context, Israel has sent messages to Lebanon that it will launch a large-scale military operation against Hezbollah terrorists, including expanding military operations into new areas, the outlet reported.
Israel may also resort to imposing an air, land, and sea blockade on Lebanon as a ramification for Beirut's failure to disarm the terror group and prevent Hezbollah from joining an escalated conflict.
Negotiations reportedly include exploring the deployment of military forces from Italy, Switzerland, and Jordan to aid in removing Hezbollah's weaponry, according to Al-Modon.
However, conditions for reaching an agreement are not in place, as Hezbollah refuses to hand over weapons, and the LAF does not want to enter into a confrontation with the Iranian proxy, the report said.
The terror group is also betting on developments in the escalated conflict in Yemen between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition forces, the report stated.
Danielle Greyman-Kennard contributed to this report.

articles.title: Letters to the editor: Readers question Trump's Russian diesel deal and US sanctions policy
articles.body:
Letters to the editor: Readers question Trump's Russian diesel deal and US sanctions policy
President Donald Trump (R) walks toward Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) to shake hands during a joint press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S. on Aug. 15, 2025. (Jae C. Hong / AP)
The Kyiv Independent Opinion Desk
This week's letters come from readers questioning the Trump administration's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel amid rising prices in the United States. An American reader argues the deal benefits Russian President Vladimir Putin at Ukraine's expense, a scholar questions whether a U.S. sanctions bill will meaningfully pressure Moscow, and a British reader raises concerns about Washington's turn to Russian oil.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to letters@kyivindependent.com — your letter may appear in our Letters section.
read also
Six days of diesel for America, and billions for Putin
Mark Cary, United States member
U.S. President Donald Trump's MAGA Republican Party is projected to lose the midterm elections in a few weeks, and much of his power and support within the government could evaporate.
Trump needs a scapegoat for the crippling rise in diesel prices in the United States. He has now decided that scapegoat will be Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The diesel "deal" Trump announced a few days ago is nothing but a calculated act of gaslighting aimed at Americans and a wholesale admission that he has always been on Team Russia.
Trump says the deal will give the United States 1.8 million tons, or 14 million barrels, of diesel over the next 90 days, with another 3 million tons next year if Russia can supply it.
This figure is so minor in real terms that it would keep American trucks and industry running on diesel for a mere six days. Donald Trump has simultaneously destroyed American credibility, sided with the enemy, and sold out Ukraine for a pittance.
read also
The US-Russia sanctions bill is not a sanctions bill
Karl Frost, United States / Germany member
The Lindsey Graham bill in the US, passed by Congress on Sept. 16, was celebrated internationally as a landmark Russian sanctions bill. Ukraine supporters who cheered this seem not to have fully appreciated that most Democrats voted against it.
Despite appearances, legally, the bill does not mandate Russia-related sanctions. The legally consequential aspect of the bill is authorizing discretionary tariff powers for the president with no meaningful oversight.
The bill identifies two categories of tariff targets: the top five importers of Russian oil and the top five facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
There is language in the bill "mandating" these tariffs. However, the bill gives the president arbitrary, discretionary powers to make exceptions. In other words, the president is not actually mandated to impose these tariffs.
Trump already had the power to sanction Russia, which he was not using, so there is no reason to think this further permission to tariff Russian oil consumers will be used, especially in light of his announcement that the U.S. would buy diesel fuel from Russia to offset fuel price increases caused by his war with Iran.
Unlike the "importer" tariffs, which do have relatively objective criteria, the "facilitator" tariffs are based on presidential interpretation. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed, for example in Dalton v. Specter, that where a statute grants such pure executive discretion as spelled out in the bill, courts will decline to review the factual basis behind the president's determination. The president could theoretically designate any nation currently locked in a trade dispute with the U.S., including allies of Ukraine, as a "facilitator of sanction evasions," slap them with 100% tariffs, and face zero judicial review.
This is the central concern raised by Democrats. As U.S. Representative Don Beyer stated, "This bill would do more harm than good for America and for Ukraine. Giving (Trump) this power when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it would be an incredible mistake."
Is there anything to do about this?
Mostly no, at least not directly, except for dropping illusions. This matters because the bill is being presented as a tool to pressure Russia and support Ukraine. Trump already declines to use his existing sanctions powers, so there is little reason to expect this one to pressure Russia, and it could actually backfire on Ukraine.
read also
The US turn to Russian oil raises questions
Barry Foster, United Kingdom member
I am a U.K. citizen living in the South West of England. I have a 23-year-old diesel car and am now paying 2 pounds per liter ($2.65).
I am appalled by the descent of the U.S. to the level of barbarism shown by its leaders: resorting to shouting down opposition when they have no reasoned argument and using personal insults against journalists who ask pertinent questions. But back to diesel.
Several weeks ago, Mr. Trump was castigating Ukraine for attacking Russian oil and petrochemical facilities. In the current circumstances, these are appropriate targets, in contrast with Russia's attacks on homes and civilian infrastructure. His "argument" was that Ukraine was causing a global diesel shortage through this strategy, while failing to acknowledge the sanctions he had imposed on Russia.
Ordinary Russians queuing for fuel learned more about their leaders' war from these shortages than from any other source. Mr. Trump had conveniently forgotten that he had contributed to the shortage by attacking Iran, which discovered it could hold the whole world to ransom by closing the Strait of Hormuz, creating shortages of all fuels and many other oil-based products.
Suddenly, Mr. Putin is America's savior, agreeing to export "millions of barrels" of oil to the US! Where has this oil appeared from? Is it the result of lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet? Is Ukraine no longer attacking Russian oil facilities? Maybe these are magic oil wells?
Any story that will last long enough for Mr. Trump to tell it to voters ahead of the midterm elections appears on his antisocial media sites.

articles.title: Kyiv stopped attacking Russia's oil refineries, Moscow continues pounding Ukraine's energy grid, Zelensky says
articles.body:
Kyiv stopped attacking Russia's oil refineries, Moscow continues pounding Ukraine's energy grid, Zelensky says
Since U.S. President Donald Trump's sudden announcement of an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, Ukraine has not targeted Russia’s oil refineries or energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13.
Russia ignored the ceasefire, Zelensky added.
"Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire. But Russia did not heed," Zelensky said on social media.
Trump made it very clear that the U.S. can influence both sides when responding to reporters' questions on why he announced a ceasefire without consulting either side.
"They agreed because I said they agreed. And that thing has to get settled."
The announcement of yet another ceasefire was news to Kyiv, but Zelensky expressed Ukraine's willingness to uphold it in an interview with Axios.
"If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia soon violated the energy ceasefire by attacking Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant in the evening of Oct.11.
Following the attack, Zelensky disclosed that over the past week, Russia has carried out over 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity and transmission facilities, in addition to 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities.
"They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded," he wrote.
On Oct. 12, Russia seemingly rejected the idea of a ceasefire. "We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in turn.
The truce also makes little sense for Ukraine if it only addresses oil refineries. Zelensky said Ukraine is "ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," but it must go beyond just oil refineries to include energy infrastructure.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago," Zelensky said on Oct. 12 in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum.
As Russia continues to pound Ukraine's energy grid, Kyiv — a city with over three million residents, comparable in population and size to Berlin — endures hour-long power outages, with some districts also being deprived of water.
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social, and his 'Shahed' drones follow a different set of instructions," Zelensky said.

articles.title: Ukraine says it hit 12 Russian refineries in September. No refinery strikes reported since Trump’s “energy ceasefire”
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces hit 12 large Russian refineries in September, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense said, according to ArmyInform on 12 October. The farthest on the ministry’s list, Lukoil’s refinery in Perm, lies about 1,500 kilometers from Ukraine’s border. Since Trump's 11 October announcement, Euromaidan Press has found no reports of new Ukrainian refinery strikes in the official and unofficial Ukrainian and Russian sources it monitors.
A refinery-for-refinery pause would limit Ukraine’s ability to disrupt Russia’s oil industry while leaving Moscow free to keep attacking Ukraine’s energy system, giving Russia an advantage in a war where both sides use energy infrastructure as a target. The issue has become urgent since Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October, after which Ukraine reported holding off strikes on Russian energy facilities while Zelenskyy said Russia attacked several Ukrainian energy sites.
The campaign continued into October. Ukraine’s General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck the Samara oil pumping station overnight into 10 October, the third attack on the station that month, according to Radio Svoboda.
Ukraine held off, Russia hit six energy sites
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight on 11–12 October following Trump's announcement. Monitoring channels and official Russian sources did not report any new refinery strikes on 13 October.
“Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on the territory of Russia because President Trump said that there would be an energy ceasefire,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
He added that Ukraine does not announce its next operational steps. Zelenskyy said Russia attacked six Ukrainian energy facilities on 12 October alone, according to Radio Svoboda.
Refineries first, power plants possibly later
A White House official told Axios that the proposal would begin with both sides halting attacks on oil refineries, with a possible agreement covering power plants to follow. Axios reported that Russia had not accepted a ceasefire.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the proposal, as described, would give Russia a major concession without offering Ukraine anything in return: Russia has scores of operating refineries, while Ukraine has one. ISW also said the proposal would allow Russia to continue its winter strikes on Ukrainian power stations.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Iskander-M Repair Base, Threatening Its Ballistic Missile Operations
articles.body:

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Iskander-M Repair Base, Threatening Its Ballistic Missile Operations
Ukrainian forces struck a repair base for Iskander-M missile systems, a radar station, logistics sites, and Russian troop concentrations on October 12 and overnight into October 13.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine announced the strikes on October 13, noting that several Russian military facilities were hit in Russia and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The confirmed targets included:
- a repair base near Kondrinka in Russia’s Kursk region servicing Iskander-M self-propelled launchers and transporter-loader vehicles;
- a Russian radar station near Skryabine in Russia’s Bryansk region;
- a fuel and lubricants depot near Dovzhansk in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- an ammunition depot near Rubizhne in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region;
- Russian troop concentrations near Selydove, Rozdolne, Suzhenka, and Myrnohrad in the Donetsk region;
- Russian personnel near Naberezhne in the Zaporizhzhia region and Kuzemivka in the Luhansk region.
The Iskander-M is a Russian mobile short-range ballistic missile system designed to strike high-value targets behind the front line. Its launchers and support vehicles allow Russian units to relocate quickly and conduct missile strikes from dispersed positions.
Damage to a repair base can reduce the availability of launchers and support vehicles by disrupting maintenance and the return of damaged equipment to service. The General Staff did not disclose the extent of the damage or Russian losses from the strikes.
Days earlier, Ukraine struck a similar set of Russian maintenance and supply sites across the temporarily occupied east.
Strikes on October 10 and overnight into October 11 hit a military repair unit near Chystiakove, also known as Torez, and logistics facilities near Makiivka and Horodyshche. Russian troop concentrations near Purdivka, Lysychansk, and Irmino were also targeted.
Earlier on October 10, Ukrainian forces hit command posts in the Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk regions, an electronic warfare station in Russia's Bryansk region, and a repair base near Sukhodilsk.

articles.title: USA and Europe drafting peace plan for Ukraine and Russia involving security guarantees and territorial compromise – media
articles.body:
The USA and European countries are developing a peace initiative to end Russia's war against Ukraine; the plan entails funding for Ukraine's reconstruction, security guarantees, economic cooperation with Russia, and a ceasefire along the current front line, The Washington Post reports, citing a US official familiar with the negotiations.
According to the ezine, the diplomatic push came during a six-hour meeting last Friday in Florida hosted by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. The meeting, which included Ukrainian officials and representatives of Britain, France and Germany, was held at the Shell Bay Golf Club, a development owned by Witkoff in Hallandale Beach.
According to the Washington Post, U.S. negotiators are trying to frame a package that addresses Ukraine’s and Russia’s postwar needs in a way that ends the bloodbath and leaves both countries better off — as a sweetener for a territorial compromise neither side will like.
“We need to make the problem and the solution bigger to help both sides see what the postwar situation would be — and then make concessions,” the publication quoted an American official as saying.
The peace plan comprises four main components. Ukraine’s reconstruction would be the first pillar. The World Bank and the investment firm BlackRock want to create a framework for meeting Zelensky’s myriad cash needs — for rebuilding the devastated areas of the country, providing benefits to families of dead and wounded soldiers, and restoring a shattered economy.
Security guarantees would be the second essential component. Ukraine would get a pledge from the United States and European nations that they would respond militarily if Russia attacked again, which the U.S. official described as equivalent to NATO’s Article 5. The official said Russia would also negotiate agreements with Europe that would address its security concerns, though it’s not clear what this would involve.
A third pillar would be economic integration of Russia, Ukraine and Europe through an energy deal. One aspect might be a pipeline carrying Russian oil and gas to Europe, with Ukraine and Russia splitting the profits. Such a pipeline could sharply reduce European energy costs, the official said. In addition to providing Russia with “long-term access to the European energy market,” a peace deal would specify how and when existing economic sanctions would be removed. The final, the fourth, piece of the deal would be the most unpalatable. Russia, which began the war hoping to conquer all of Ukraine, would agree to a ceasefire along the existing front line, or “line of control,” as negotiators describe it. For Ukraine, that would mean allowing Russia to control the territory it occupies — including the bitterly contested area known as Donbas. One hurdle is that the line of control is fuzzy, given small shifts in the front almost every day.
According to a European diplomat, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries are affecting Russia's economy and strengthening Ukraine's negotiating position.
“Clearly, the Ukrainians’ ability to strike refineries is having impact on Russia’s economy. It has increased Zelenskyy’s leverage,” the European diplomat is quoted by the publication as saying.

articles.title: Poland called on Europe to switch to a "war footing" due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
articles.body:
Poland called on Europe to switch to a "war footing" due to the pace of weapons production in the russian federation
Kyiv • UNN
Poland's Minister of Defence called on Europe to sharply increase the production of weapons and ammunition. russia is outpacing the EU in terms of arms production.
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that Europe must accelerate the production of ammunition and weapons in order not to fall behind Russia’s pace. He warned that failure to do so would have negative consequences for Europe. Euronews reports, writes UNN.
I am actually in favour of a wartime footing when it comes to production in the defence sector. That is exactly how the Russian Federation is operating now. We cannot ignore this fact
Russia switched to wartime production in the defence sector even before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. According to forecasts, in 2026 it will spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on the armed forces.
According to a recent report by Estonian intelligence, in 2025 Russia produced approximately seven million artillery, mortar, tank and missile munitions. Russian forces are currently using approximately 10,000–15,000 munitions daily, continuing their aggression against Ukraine.
By contrast, Europe’s defence industry suffered from insufficient funding and fragmentation for decades.
Russia is outproducing the EU in terms of ammunition production. According to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness, the 27 EU member states and Norway are expected to produce only two million 150 mm artillery shells this year.
The efforts of European countries and NATO members to rearm have delivered the largest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, total defence spending by EU member states in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of the European Union’s combined GDP, the report says.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said that it was “time” for Europe to prepare to defend itself independently by significantly increasing production in the defence sector.
He warned that failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, adding: “This is one of the shortcomings, but in the future it will also have a negative impact on us and future generations.”
As the publication notes, Poland is among the countries that spend the largest share of GDP on defence capabilities. According to US representative to NATO Matthew Whitaker, the country allocates 4.7% of its GDP to core defence needs.

articles.title: Houthis and Saudis strike each other in latest escalation
articles.body:
Houthis and Saudis show no intent to stop fighting
October 13, 2026
Iran-backed Houthi rebels on Tuesday said that Saudi Arabia had carried out overnight airstrikes targeting border regions in Yemen.
Rebel-run satellite television said two strikes had hit the Red Sea island of Kamaran and a third targeted Qanawis, north of Hodeida port.
Further strikes were reported in Jawf and rebels said their forces had downed a Saudi drone over Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
The strikes came just hours after air-raid sirens blared and loud explosions were heard in the Saudi capital Riyadh, which has come under intense fire for the past several days as fighting between the two belligerents intensifies.
The Houthis have clashed with Saudi Arabia since the kingdom stepped into Yemen's civil war to lead a military coalition against the Iran-backed fighters in 2015.
The rebels have pounded Saudi Arabia in recent days, repeatedly attacking the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. On Saturday, one of those attacks killed 13 people in what was the deadliest in the country in over a decade.
On Tuesday, Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for an immediate end to Houthi attacks on the kingdom, telling Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi that there is "no justification for these attacks and they cannot be accepted."
Houthi attacks' economic impact on Saudi Arabia
Beyond reigniting fighting tied to Yemen's civil war, increased Houthi activity has come as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran, launched on February 28.
A regional proxy, the Houthis have helped Iran further destabilize the region by striking largely at the oil and transport infrastructure that brings oil and gas from US allies in the gulf to market.
Saudi Arabia is the world's top oil exporter and Houthi attacks have not only raised security issues, they have greatly hampered the kingdom's ability to get its product to market.
In its latest annual World Economic Outlook, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates Saudi GDP will contract by 3.3% on the year as a result, with Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz compounded by Houthi maneuvering in the Red Sea and attacks on Saudi oil refineries and tankers.
Saudi Arabia quickly diverted oil exports away from Hormuz as Iran's blockade dragged on, making use instead, of its overland pipelines and Red Sea access. Houthi attacks, however, have also dramatically impacted these.
Saudi Arabia stops issuing air raids
The devastation of the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia have prompted the kingdom to seek help from Washington and US President Donald Trump.
Although he previously ignored Saudi requests for assistance, on Saturday Trump mused about joining the fight against the rebels.
News of this consideration drew a quick response from the Houthis, with a representative saying US interests in the region would be targeted should DC enter the fray.
Despite at least 18 people being killed and more than 300 injured in recent days, Saudi Arabia has stopped issuing air raid alerts in the kingdom.
The government has not spoken of the policy change but observers suggest it may be an effort to avoid stirring public panic as the country's security vulnerabilities come into focus.
Still, analysts warn that the change could have the opposite effect by amplifying uncertainty over the current situation.
Last week, prior to a string of airport attacks, government officials said the alerts had been halted due to citizens' complaints about being woken by them.
Further, Saudi government officials on Monday reminded residents of regulations issued in March that forbid sharing any images related to Houthi air attacks, including missile interceptions or impact craters.
Former US Ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney told Reuters news agency that Riyadh — which initiated public warnings in May before halting them on September 29 — was trying to balance public messaging with efforts to prevent disruption in the kingdom but that in his opinion leaders had ended up adding to a sense of unease about Houthi airstrikes.

articles.title: Gazan families fight to protect slain journalists' legacies
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
'Killed twice': Gaza families fight to clear the names of journalists branded militants by Israel
"Publishing my son’s name on that list is a second assassination," begins 70-year-old Bakr al-Louh. "The first time, they killed his body. Now they are killing his legacy and his career as a journalist. They are killing him in his grave."
His son, Ahmed al-Louh, was a photojournalist working for Al Jazeera. He was 39 when an Israeli strike hit a civil defence post in Nuseirat refugee camp, in central Gaza, on 15 December 2024. He had returned there shortly before, after filming ambulances carrying the bodies of people killed in an earlier Israeli strike nearby.
On 1 October, the family found Ahmed’s name and photograph in The Press Files, an online database published by the Israeli occupation. It names 170 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed in Gaza and claims they were members or fighters of armed factions.
"This news destroyed us," his father says. He says the allegations against Ahmed are "lies, with no basis in truth."
Ahmed’s page on the site lists him as a military operative in Hamas’s armed wing. When The New Arab viewed it on 11 October, it contained no supporting evidence. Its only image linked to an internal address and did not load.
The Israeli army claims the database is the product of an in-depth investigation, drawing on open-source information, documents seized in Gaza, interrogations of alleged militants and intelligence gathered during military operations.
But the evidence it presents varies widely, from cropped documents to old photographs.
In 49 cases, the main evidence is an obituary published by an armed group. An analysis by +972 Magazine found that 59 of the pages contain no evidence at all, only a line saying the claim is based on intelligence sources.
For Bakr al-Louh, the list is an extension of the war on Gaza’s journalists. Targeting them, he says, is "an attempt to silence the free word and the truth, because the occupation doesn’t want any voice or image to come out of Gaza that exposes its massacres."
The fear does not stop with the dead. "We have a real fear that these accusations will reach the rest of the family," he tells The New Arab. If any of them needs urgent medical treatment outside Gaza, he worries Israel could reject them on security grounds.
‘He moved in the open’
Ahmed Khaireddine, 30, was a cameraman for Al-Quds Al-Youm. He was killed on 27 December 2023, when an Israeli strike hit his home in Beit Lahia, in northern Gaza. His uncle Mohammed Khaireddine, a journalist with Al-Aqsa TV, died with him, along with 23 other members of the family.
The Press Files describes Ahmed as an Islamic Jihad commander and lists his employer as Al-Aqsa TV, the channel his uncle worked for. His brother Basel, 36, a journalist himself, says the photograph on the page is fabricated. He says he had never seen it in his life. He believes the way his brother died is the clearest proof the allegations are false.
"Before he was killed, Ahmed spent more than 80 days moving around with his camera and his blue vest, covering al-Shifa and the Indonesian hospitals," he tells The New Arab.
"If he had really been a military target, they would have picked him off in the streets and public squares, where he moved openly. But he was killed with his family, in a massacre that destroyed three adjoining houses at once and killed more than 30 civilians."
Many of the names on the list, he says, belong to colleagues he saw every day. "We saw them all the time where journalists gathered at hospitals and out in the field, and we never once saw them among gunmen or fighters. They were doing their work in the open, and the drones above them knew very well they were civilians doing their jobs," Basel says.
He says Israel is deliberately confusing political affiliation with combat. "A Palestinian is born with a political affiliation. That is nothing shameful, and it does not take a journalist out of the civilian work protected under international law."
'A ready-made warrant'
Photojournalist Bilal Abu Samak says the database’s real purpose is to justify the killing of journalists who covered the war. He and Mohammed both describe the accusations as a ready-made warrant, one that could be used against journalists who are still alive and still reporting.
Gaza’s journalists, Abu Samak says, are civilians who wear protective vests and carry no weapons.
"Through this list, they are trying to terrify us and force us to abandon journalism, especially as they keep barring international journalists from entering Gaza to document their violations," he says.
"We demand real protection for press crews, and that the professional legacy of our colleagues who were killed be preserved."
Israel has barred foreign reporters from Gaza since the start of the war, apart from brief visits escorted by the army, and denies deliberately targeting journalists.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) told The New Arab it was still reviewing all the claims in the database. When new information emerges about the killing of a journalist anywhere in the world, it said, it reviews each case independently and updates its records.
CPJ published the database a week after completing its own review.
On 24 September, the New York-based group removed 22 people from its list of journalists killed in Israel and the Occupied Palestinian Territory. It found that 19 of them had been militants or had taken part in combat, and that three could not be confirmed as journalists.
CPJ now counts 191 Palestinian journalists and media workers killed by Israeli forces. It said Israeli forces remain responsible for the large majority of journalist killings worldwide since 2023, and that each case in its review required interviews with at least two independent, credible sources as well as desk research.
The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate puts the toll higher, at more than 260. Its secretary-general, Ahed Farawneh, says the timing of the Israeli database is no accident.
"The occupation is trying to get around the huge numbers of journalists killed by levelling these false accusations of links to armed groups," he says, "to justify targeting them after a global outcry and strong condemnation from journalists’ unions and international organisations."
When the syndicate looks at the lives of those killed, he says, it finds that "they were working under the sun," in plain sight and far from any armed faction.
The syndicate says it applies criteria matching those of the International Federation of Journalists before recognising anyone as a journalist killed in the line of duty.
It is also building a case file of killings, injuries, arrests, destroyed offices and homes, and families wiped out and documenting the ban on foreign press and on bringing cameras and equipment into Gaza.
"We have obtained power of attorney from the families of those killed, and from injured journalists and former detainees, to file cases at the International Criminal Court," Ahed says.
"Unfortunately, the court is still stalling on opening this file. But together with the International Federation of Journalists, we insist on it, and on the families’ right to take the occupation to court."
He points to earlier legal efforts over the killings of journalists Shireen Abu Akleh, Ahmed Abu Hussein and Yaser Murtaja. The syndicate is also working with rights groups and legal experts to bring cases in countries whose laws allow prosecution of war crimes committed abroad.
'In case of doubt'
Hussein Hammad, a specialist in media and human rights, says the database deliberately blurs the line between political or institutional affiliation and taking a direct part in hostilities.
Working for a media outlet linked to a political faction, or sympathising with one, does not strip a journalist of civilian protection, he says.
International humanitarian law is clear on this. Article 79 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions states that journalists on dangerous professional missions in armed conflict are civilians and must be protected as such.
Under Article 51, civilians lose that protection only "for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities." Article 50 adds that "in case of doubt whether a person is a civilian, that person shall be considered to be a civilian."
Accusing journalists after they have been killed, with no chance to answer the charges, has no legal value, Hammad says, and amounts to a cover for extrajudicial killing.
International justice, he adds, does not accept military verdicts based on evidence the victim or their lawyer can never see or challenge. He says the response must be to document every violation, gather physical evidence and build cases for court.
For Bakr al-Louh, the fight is also about memory. His son’s last assignment was to document the dead of Nuseirat being carried to hospital. Shortly afterwards, he was among them.
Ismail Nofal is a Gaza-based journalist specialising in human interest stories

articles.title: NATO exercise involves potential countries for nuclear weapons deployment — expert

MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. According to Stepanov, the exercise aims to ensure coordination during strategic operations, primarily involving the air force component. "These maneuvers involve 60 aircraft to provide both strategic reconnaissance capabilities and cover for the main delivery systems as part of a combined nuclear-use scenario across various sectors," the expert added.
Starting October 13, NATO is conducting nuclear deterrence exercises in Italy without the use of live munitions. Seventeen nations are participating, the NATO press service reported. It emphasized that "no live weapons are used in Steadfast Noon. The exercise is not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country."
The Steadfast Noon exercise is held annually as "part of NATO’s efforts to maintain readiness and test procedures that contribute to the Alliance’s deterrence and defense." It involves dual-capable aircraft designed to carry both conventional and nuclear munitions.

articles.title: Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Iran pledges stronger deterrence, asserts sovereignty over Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN— Iranian military officials have reaffirmed the country’s determination to strengthen its defense capabilities, protect its maritime interests and oppose efforts to restore a US-dominated security order in West Asia, arguing that regional stability must be based on national sovereignty and cooperation among neighboring countries.
The statements by senior military figures and defense officials address several interconnected issues, including Iran’s military preparedness following recent hostilities, the strategic management of the Strait of Hormuz, the future of regional security arrangements and the growing controversy over Washington’s use of historical and civilizational rhetoric in its confrontation with Iran.
Military preparedness and deterrence
Iranian military officials say the country has drawn lessons from recent conflicts and strengthened its ability to respond to potential threats.
Rear Admiral Bemani, deputy commander of the Iranian Army’s Navy, said Iran had studied its adversaries’ weaknesses and developed new weapons and tactics considering recent military confrontations.
He said the Iranian Army’s Navy, working alongside Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy, had inflicted significant blows on US forces at certain stages of the fighting. According to Bemani, US forces are now operating farther from Iran’s maritime borders than in previous periods.
He warned that any renewed miscalculation would prompt a response from Iran’s Navy and could force hostile forces to move farther away from the country’s maritime borders.
Bemani also distinguished between the responsibilities of the armed forces and those of the government in addressing the US naval blockade. While the government handles its political and economic dimensions, he said, the military remains focused on resistance, defense preparedness and responding to threats.
Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza has likewise emphasized the importance of strengthening Iran’s scientific, industrial and defense capabilities. He said national security requires the means to defend the country’s sovereignty and ensure that the armed forces are adequately equipped to protect Iran.
The emphasis on domestic capabilities reflects the Iranian military leadership’s stated position that deterrence depends not only on weapons and operational readiness but also on scientific advancement, industrial capacity and the ability to adapt to evolving military threats.
Strait of Hormuz: Strategic management and maritime sovereignty
The Strait of Hormuz remains another central element of Iran’s security calculations, given its geographical position and importance to global energy supplies.
Major General Yahya Rahim Safavi, head of the Lt. Gen. Qassem Soleimani Research Institute of Sacred Defense Sciences and Teachings, has identified the strategic management of the waterway as a key component of Iran’s approach to countering the US naval blockade.
Safavi said Iran’s geographical position and rights as a coastal state underpin its authority to safeguard its interests in the strait and surrounding waters. He stressed that exercising sovereignty should not automatically be interpreted as an intention to escalate tensions.
He also distinguished between closing the waterway and managing maritime traffic, arguing that these are fundamentally different approaches. In his assessment, the transport of military equipment that directly threatens Iran’s national security could make the management or restriction of maritime traffic a strategic necessity.
Safavi added that alternative pipelines do not eliminate the Strait of Hormuz’s importance to international energy markets.
According to the US Energy Information Administration, approximately 20 million barrels of oil and petroleum liquids passed through the strait daily in 2022, accounting for roughly one-fifth of global petroleum liquids consumption. The waterway is also a major route for liquefied natural gas shipments, making its security a matter of international economic significance.
Iranian officials maintain that maritime security cannot be separated from the wider political and military circumstances in the region. From their perspective, the management of the strait must take account of Iran’s sovereignty, the security threats it faces and the need to protect vital national interests.
Safavi has also presented Iran’s approach as part of a broader response to maritime pressure and sanctions, while arguing that regional security should be pursued through the participation of countries in the area.
Tehran rejects a US-led security order
Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi, spokesperson for Iran’s Armed Forces, has said Iran will not allow the regional order envisaged by the United States and Israel to be restored in West Asia.
Shekarchi called on neighboring countries to reconsider their reliance on an ineffective US security umbrella. He argued that recent conflicts had demonstrated the risks of depending on Washington for regional protection.
He accused the United States of fuel smuggling, maritime theft and psychological warfare surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, adding that political statements and media messaging could not change realities on the ground. He also questioned Washington’s ability to guarantee regional security and urged neighboring governments not to base their security calculations on the policies of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
 
Shekarchi said Iran’s armed forces were more capable than before and remained prepared to defend the country against threats.
The statements reflect Tehran’s long-standing emphasis on regional participation in security arrangements. Iranian officials argue that countries sharing West Asia’s geographical and strategic environment should play the leading role in maintaining its stability rather than relying on military structures dominated by outside powers.
In this view, regional cooperation is not merely a diplomatic preference, but a security requirement shaped by geography, shared interests and the consequences of military confrontation.
Civilizational confrontation and Washington’s historical rhetoric
Alongside the military and strategic debate, Iranian officials have strongly criticized the use of historical and civilizational references in contemporary political disputes.
Caretaker Defense Minister Ebn al-Reza condemned remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens that invoked the ancient conflicts between Greece and Persia. He warned against turning historical and cultural differences into a basis for present-day political or military confrontation.
“Civilizational confrontation is playing with fire,” Ebn al-Reza said, cautioning that those who ignite such tensions may not be able to control their consequences.
He stressed that Iran possesses an ancient civilization and a distinct national identity that do not depend on external recognition. He also argued that the country must strengthen its scientific, industrial and defense capabilities to safeguard its independence.
Brigadier General Ali Balali, an adviser to the commander of the IRGC Aerospace Force, offered a broader ideological interpretation of the confrontation. He said the United States and Israel sought to exploit the wealth and resources of Eastern countries while preventing the emergence of a new Islamic civilization.
“Civilization belongs to the East, and they have no civilization of their own,” Balali said.
He urged neighboring Muslim countries to be aware of efforts by Washington and its allies to prevent the peoples of the East and the Muslim world from becoming more capable and prosperous. Balali also criticized the historical record of Western powers, citing the mass killing of Indigenous peoples in the Americas and violence against populations in Africa.
He maintained that Western powers would ultimately fail to prevent the emergence of a global order shaped by Islamic civilization.
The controversy has also drawn attention to Trump’s statements during the war against Iran. On April 1, he threatened to bombard Iran and said US forces would “bring them back to the stone ages,” while also threatening Iranian power plants and other infrastructure. On April 7, he warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again” if Iran failed to meet his demands.
The remarks have become part of the wider dispute over the language used to describe the conflict and its potential consequences. Iranian officials have argued that such rhetoric cannot be separated from threats against the country’s infrastructure, population and sovereignty.
The exchange has also revived historical references on both sides. Iranian political figures have invoked episodes from the country’s past, including the capture of Roman Emperor Valerian by the Sasanian king Shapur I in 260 AD, in response to Washington’s references to ancient Greco-Persian wars.
For Iranian officials, the issue extends beyond competing interpretations of history. They frame it as a broader question of who has the authority to define civilization, determine the political future of other societies and shape the emerging international order.
Taken together, the statements by Iran’s defense and military officials present a unified message: the country intends to strengthen its deterrent capabilities, safeguard its sovereign interests in strategically important waters and resist external efforts to determine the future of West Asia. In their assessment, lasting regional stability requires respect for national sovereignty and a greater role for regional countries in shaping their own security arrangements, rather than renewed dependence on outside military powers.

articles.title: Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Putin-Trump deal about ‘much more’ than diesel – Serbia’s Vucic to RT (VIDEO)
US President Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia is part of a broader geopolitical strategy to draw Moscow away from Beijing, Aleksandar Vucic has told RT Balkan in an exclusive interview.
According to Vucic, who recently stepped down as Serbian president to run for prime minister, Washington, which sees China as its main rival, hopes to weaken Beijing’s partnership with Russia by improving ties with Moscow.
Trump announced the deal following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on October 9. Moscow agreed to release more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and one million tons thereafter. Washington subsequently waived sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.
Ahead of the deal, Trump blamed soaring fuel prices on Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries, although markets have also been disrupted by the US war with Iran, which has affected shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
“As far as Donald Trump is concerned, he is doing a smart thing for America, he is trying to do something to bring down the price per gallon… But I don’t think this is just about diesel,” Vucic said, noting that the initial 300,000 tons would cover less than a day’s US consumption.
With the US midterms approaching and Trump’s standoff with Tehran increasingly unpopular, Vucic suggested the deal could partly be aimed at winning over voters by lowering fuel prices. However, he suggested there was a larger geopolitical calculation behind the agreement.
“I think it is about something much more than this. Donald Trump knows that his main competitor is China. And is trying, in a sophisticated way, to move Russia somewhat away from China and bring it closer to the US.”
Asked whether Trump was seeking closer ties with Moscow, Vucic replied: “Of course.”
“If he is in conflict with Russia, he will only push Russia closer to China,” he explained. “Trump is trying, I assume, to draw Russia, China’s powerful and strong ally, at least a little away from that alliance.”
The Trump administration has long treated China as a major strategic rival. Its 2025 National Security Strategy calling for a rebalancing of economic ties with Beijing. Trump nevertheless hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington last month for talks on trade, Taiwan and Iran. The two sides agreed to extend their trade truce until January, but tensions over tariffs, technology and security persist.
Russia and China, meanwhile, have only deepened their strategic and energy cooperation in light of Ukraine-related Western sanctions on Moscow. Beijing has become Moscow’s biggest oil customer and a major buyer of Russian gas, with supplies expanding through the Power of Siberia pipeline as Russia redirected energy exports away from Europe.
Talking about Russia-US ties, Vucic also pointed to Washington’s diplomatic push to resolve the Ukraine conflict, saying its parallel negotiating channels with Moscow and Kiev show it is serious about reaching a settlement. However, he sees little prospect of an imminent breakthrough.
Vucic expressed hope that a peace deal could be reached within five to six months. Asked whether he fears that the conflict could evolve into a direct confrontation between Russia and the EU, Vucic replied: “I fear that, but I hope it won’t happen.”
Serbia has maintained close ties with Russia and, under Vucic, has resisted EU pressure to impose sanctions on Moscow over Ukraine, despite Belgrade’s ambitions to join the bloc. In the interview, Vucic again stressed the need to preserve Serbia’s traditional ties with Moscow despite external pressure, saying leaders must “keep a cool head and make rational and wise decisions.”
Vucic resigned during his second presidential term last month ahead of snap parliamentary elections scheduled for October 25. Barred by the Serbian constitution from seeking a third term, he is now seeking the prime minister’s post as a candidate for the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

articles.title: “We don’t need to hit the entire plant”—Ukraine’s drones go for refinery parts sanctions make hard to repair
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones have helped push Russia into its worst fuel crisis since the Soviet Union fell, The Washington Post (WaPo) reported on 11 October.
Diesel is where this war reaches American drivers. US President Donald Trump blames rising diesel prices mostly on Russia’s war in Ukraine, while experts blame mainly the US war with Iran. Some of his allies now accuse Kyiv of trying to sway the US midterms.
Drones go for the first stage of refining
The Washington Post looked at dozens of strikes between 1 April and 31 August. Three refinery experts then examined satellite images of 54 strikes with visible damage. In over half, the damage seems to be to the desalting and distillation units, known by the Russian acronym ELOU-AVT. These units clean the crude of water and salt, then split it into separate compounds, the first steps toward gasoline and diesel. More than a third appear to have hit secondary units, which turn those compounds into jet fuel, gasoline, and liquefied petroleum gas.
From April through August, drones struck two-thirds or more of the 36 big Russian refineries that S&P Global Energy tracks, a strike every third day. Some took as many as five hits. On 16 June, drones set the Moscow refinery’s distillation towers on fire. That strike and a second one days later kept the plant offline into September, WaPo reported, citing data firm Kpler. Ukraine targeted the refinery again on 20 September.
Trump’s Russian diesel deal, which drew fury in Ukraine, is unlikely to lower prices, experts say
“We don’t need to hit the entire plant,” a Ukrainian drone battalion commander with the call sign Tango told The Washington Post. Ukraine knows where to strike so that a refinery stops and stays down, he said. His unit, Ukraine’s 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Systems, runs long-range strikes deep inside Russia.
Sanctions slow the repairs
The EU banned exports of oil-refining equipment to Russia the day after the 2022 invasion, and the US followed days later. WaPo reported that the bans cover the distillation and secondary processing units Ukraine keeps hitting. The bans make spare parts hard to get, Alexander Kolyandr of Eurasia Group told the paper, and the strikes come faster than repairs.
Since last year, Ukraine has doubled the size of each wave, decoys included, a person involved in the strike campaign told WaPo. The decoys are unarmed and draw Russian fire, wasting air-defense ammunition, WaPo explained. Without them, the person said, Ukraine would simply lose expensive systems. András Rácz of the German Council on Foreign Relations told WaPo that even if only 2–3% of drones get through, the damage is significant.

articles.title: Germany detains two Turkish nationals suspected of torching a Polish Starlink station that helps route internet to Ukraine
articles.body:
German services detained two Turkish citizens on 12 October over the 23 September arson attack on a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska, near Warsaw, Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) said. Both are suspected of arson, and Polish officials blame Russian intelligence. RMF24 later reported that German police also detained two more people who may be connected to the attack.
Poland is one of the main corridors for Western aid to Ukraine, and Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski has said Poland spends about $50 million a year on Ukraine's Starlink service. That puts Polish infrastructure in the path of a Russian campaign that already hacks cameras to track arms heading east.
Fingerprints, DNA, and a route out
The men were held under European arrest warrants and now await transfer to Poland. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote that the suspects would face charges of “subversion, sabotage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service” after their transfer to Poland. Polish authorities issued European arrest warrants for the suspects, who were subsequently detained in Germany.
Police chief Marek Boroń said investigators reconstructed how the suspects prepared the attack and fled. “We have secured recordings pointing to this specific action. We have fingerprints, the perpetrators’ DNA, how they moved, when they came to Poland, and when they were evacuated from our country,” he said. One suspect lives in Germany, and the other had been ordered to leave the country, he added.
Warsaw points at Moscow
Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the fire another act of Russia's hybrid war and promised the saboteurs will answer to Polish justice.
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” said Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Poland’s special services.
Those services increasingly turn to people tied to the criminal world, he added.
Two more possible links
German counterterrorism officers detained a woman in Berlin, and a man is also in German custody, Polish radio RMF FM reported, citing its reporter. Both may be linked to the arson. The woman allegedly picked up the Turkish men near Łódź after they entered Poland from Germany, then drove them to Wola Krobowska. The man’s role is still being examined.

Russia attacks Ukraine with ballistic missiles, Banderol drone missiles and 108 drones: air defences downs 88 UAVs
Russia attacked Ukraine with five ballistic missiles, nine drone-launched missiles and 108 drones on the night of 12-13 October. Air defence forces have destroyed or jammed 88 UAVs.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: From 18:00 on 12 October, the Russians used five Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles launched from Russia's Bryansk Oblast, nine Banderol/Dan-T drone missiles and 108 Shahed and Gerbera attack drones, as well as Parodiya decoy UAVs. Seventy-four of the drones were jet-powered.
The drones were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Kursk and Primorsko-Akhtarsk, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea.
Early reports indicated that as of 08:00, Ukrainian air defence forces had destroyed or jammed 88 drones (58 jet-powered).

In addition, drone missiles struck the city of Kharkiv, although some of them failed to reach their targets."
Details: Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.

articles.title: Russia funnels nearly half its budget into defence, cutting social spending
articles.body:
Russia’s 2027 draft budget allocates a record share to defence and security, as regions quietly divert funds for foster children and orphans to war payments and “coffin money” for soldiers’ families is cut by up to 95% in some areas.
Russia's parliament will vote later this month on a budget that allocates a record 44% of federal spending to defence and security — double the share for social programmes — as the Kremlin presses ahead with a fifth year of all-out war in Ukraine.
The State Duma, Russia's lower house of parliament, is due to begin examining the 2027–2029 draft on 22 October.
President Vladimir Putin's United Russia party won an absolute constitutional majority in September's parliamentary elections, making major amendments unlikely before it passes.
Military expenditure this year has reached 17 trillion roubles (€181 billion) against the 12.1 trillion (€129 billion) originally budgeted, showing the escalating cost of the full-scale invasion Russia launched against Ukraine in February 2022. Defence and security's 44% share of the 2027 budget is the highest on record.
The Finance Ministry's draft lists "fulfilling social obligations to citizens" as its top priority. The figures tell a different story. Social policy spending will fall 7% in 2027, from 7.1 trillion roubles (€76 billion) to 6.65 trillion (€71 billion), covering pensions, payments to veterans, maternity benefits and other support.
The government has pledged to index these payments against inflation. Russia's official inflation rate has exceeded 8% for much of the past two years, and independent economists put the real figure higher.
The Kremlin has announced a 10 trillion rouble (€107 billion) "children's budget" over the next three years, covering maternity payments, child benefits, and housing programmes. The ratio of those funds to defence spending is one to five.
Federal payments to servicemen and their families fall under the "national defence" section, whose spending will rise by roughly a quarter next year.
War at the expense of orphans and the poor
The federal budget is not the only source of pressure on social spending. Russia's regions partly fund war-related payments, many of which are already running deficits, forcing local authorities to cut civilian budgets.
In late September the Arkhangelsk region redirected more than 63 million roubles originally earmarked for social support — two-thirds from payments to foster parents, the rest from support for large families — to one-off war payments and death compensation.
A few days earlier the Tula region cut 54 million roubles from spending on foster children, low-income households, families with disabled children, housing repairs for orphans and support for labour veterans, redirecting the sum to servicemen's pay and compensation for the dead.
In St Petersburg, authorities have prepared a bill reducing spending on education, transport repairs and medical projects while increasing payments to servicemen.
'Coffin money' being cut
Regional lump-sum death payments — known informally as "coffin money" — have been cut across Russia since autumn of last year.
The payments are regional supplements to the federal one-time compensation paid to families of troops killed in action, and regions sharply raised them in 2022–2023 as they competed to attract recruits.
In Ulyanovsk region the payment stood at 1 million roubles (€10,700). By February it had been halved, then cut again to 50,000 roubles (€533).
In Bashkortostan, the initial 2 million roubles (€21,300) payment has fallen to no more than 100,000 (€1,100).
Kirov and Omsk regions have halved payments from 1 million to 500,000 roubles (€5,300). In Kemerovo the payment went down from 3 million to 1 million. In Saratov, families who received 1 million roubles until late September now receive a tenth of that.
The sums attracted fraud. In Primorsky Krai, a warrant officer was alleged to have arranged marriages between contract soldiers heading to the front and local women, with the compensation shared among participants if the men were killed.
In Khabarovsk, authorities detained six people in February on suspicion of orchestrating similar arrangements, using notarised powers of attorney to access soldiers’ bank accounts, with alleged damages reaching 2.4 million roubles (€25,600).
Some families receive nothing at all. Soldiers classified by the military as missing or as deserters rather than confirmed dead are ineligible for the one-time payment. Relatives of those killed say the designation is used to withhold compensation.
Healthcare insignificant
Healthcare spending will fall to 7 trillion roubles (€75 billion) next year, a 6.8% reduction according to calculations by independent Russian media, though the Finance Ministry disputes the figure.
Over the three-year period, healthcare will receive 28.6 trillion roubles (€305 billion) against 50 trillion roubles (€533 billion) for the military.
Funding for ambulance services has been cut by more than a quarter. The programme to build and repair outpatient clinics in the regions has been halved.
The national cancer programme will receive 3.9 billion roubles in 2027, down from 44.9 billion this year.

articles.title: British tanker completes fourteen missions in Saudi deployment
articles.body:
A Royal Air Force Voyager sent to Saudi Arabia to provide air-to-air refuelling has already flown fourteen operational missions, alongside air defence also deployed by Britain, the Prime Minister told the House of Commons.
Andy Burnham set out the deployment in a statement on the United Nations General Assembly and the international meetings that followed it, describing the Middle East as one of the subjects he had discussed with President Trump in New York.
He said: “I confirmed Britain’s decision to send air defence and a Voyager aircraft to Saudi Arabia to provide air to air refuelling support. I can confirm today it has already completed 14 operational missions. This support is needed to protect civilians. I condemn the appalling attacks on the King Khalid International Airport. We will continue to stand with Saudi Arabia against the Houthis.”
The deployment was agreed in late September in response to a Saudi request, with the Prime Minister acting on the advice of the Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting, and the Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband. Mr Burnham said then that Britain was acting to secure the interests of this country and the wider region, and that pathways needed to be kept open. Saudi Arabia was reported to be running low on interceptor stocks as Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks, which began on 8 September, continued.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh came on 8 October, when a Houthi ballistic missile killed three people, among them a Saudia pilot, Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami, and wounded dozens more, several of them foreign nationals. A Saudia aircraft was damaged. Operations at the airport have since resumed.
Attacks on Abha and King Khalid airports in early October killed three civilians and injured thirty-six, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority, and strikes on Jazan and Najran airports wounded at least three. The coalition said on 18 September that it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at King Khalid, and an explosion was heard near the airport the following day with smoke rising from a fuel storage area.
Pakistan and Turkey have agreed to deploy forces under mutual defence arrangements signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year, and a Pakistani foreign ministry spokesman has said his country now has a substantial number of forces and resources in Riyadh, acting in defence of Saudi territory without crossing into Houthi-held areas.
Voyager is the Royal Air Force’s only air-to-air refuelling aircraft and also carries the strategic air transport role, flying in two configurations, the KC Mk 2 with two underwing pods for fast jets and the KC Mk 3 with an additional centreline hose for larger aircraft.

articles.title: Defense forces strike Iskander-M repair base and radar station inside Russia – General Staff
articles.body:
Units of the Ukrainian Defense Forces struck a number of Russian military targets within Russia and in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories on Monday and overnight into Tuesday, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reports.
"A repair base for self-propelled launchers and transport-loader vehicles of the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system was struck near Kondrinka in Russia's Kursk region. Additionally, an enemy radar station was hit near the settlement of Shkryabino in Russia's Bryansk region," the General Staff said in a Telegram post.
Logistics facilities belonging to Russian units were also struck in the temporarily occupied territory of Luhansk region: a fuel and lubricant depot near Dovzhansk and an ammunition depot near Rubizhne.
"Ukrainian forces also struck areas where enemy personnel were concentrated. Concentrations of Russian troops were hit near Selydove, Razdolne, Suzhenka, and Myrnohrad in Donetsk region; Naberezhne in Zaporizhzhia region; and Kuzemivka in Luhansk region," the General Staff reported.
