articles.title: “Live long, die fast”: How Russia’s  propagandist poets try to make sense of a senseless war
articles.body:
Over the past five years, poetry by so-called “patriots of Russia” has demonstrated just how rapidly the image of the war is changing. Whereas before 2022 poetry promised a swift triumph of the Russian will, it now accustoms the reader to war as a process that can last forever. Pro-war poets claim allies wherever they can even plausibly find them — from Mozart and early 20th-century author Osip Mandelstam to the metaphorical forces of light and darkness. This hodgepodge reflects the Kremlin’s lack of coherent arguments for continuing a “special military operation” that, after nearly five years, remains nowhere close to achieving its stated objectives.
The war is short, the war is long
Over the nearly five years of full-scale war in Ukraine, neither Russian film, nor theater, nor even literature has produced any memorable works about the “special military operation.” In this respect, pro-war poetry provides the only exception — likely owing to the peculiarities of the genre. A poet is forced to be concise, and therefore more meticulous in the choice of images and words. As for the underlying messages, the pro-war poets, if they waver at all, do so in perfect alignment with the official narrative.
According to literary scholar Mikhail Edelstein, all “patriotic” poetry after Feb. 24, 2022, offers a brief recap of the events that had unfolded since 2014. Many authors who have made a name for themselves in this genre extolled, glorified, and even called for war before 2022, promising Russia a swift victory and world domination.
For example, the poem “Pre-Winter” by Igor Karaulov (from the poetry anthology “I Am the Wounded Earth: Russian Poetry on the Crimean Spring and the War in Donbas,” 2017) reflects classic dreams dating back to tsarist times:
What we will eat tomorrow,
Or how our clothes will be cut — are trifles.
Many winters passed, and we’re alive again
As long as there is vodka, Crimea, and the straits.
The word “straits” in 19th-century propaganda meant roughly what Crimea does in modern-day Russia: the epitome of the empire’s existence. The straits in question were the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, which would finally give Russia access to the southern seas. (These hopes, needless to say, have still not been realized.)
The word “straits” in 19th-century propaganda meant roughly what Crimea does in modern-day Russia: the epitome of the empire’s existence
War was expected to fulfill a range of personal hopes. Ultranationalist poet Alexander Pelevin (not to be confused with bestselling novelist Viktor Pelevin) offers his reflection on the popular expression “war will write everything off”:
War will write it all off: your debts, payments, bills,
Your deadlines, projects, books you never wrote,
A clean slate, your new chapter in life,
Last year’s draft you never meant to complete.
(2018)
“Patriots” also pinned their hopes on a war to cleanse Russian society from the “liberal delusion” of perestroika and the 1990s — along with purging culture of the much-hated “postmodernism,” which they tend to use as an umbrella term for all things alien to a patriotic heart.
“Having cleansed itself of the delusion of the liberal agenda — LGBT+, postcolonialism, radical feminism, permissiveness bordering on Satanism, and other postmodernist discourse — [poetry] has become visible again,” poet and critic Oleg Demidov writes when explaining the origin of pro-war poetry.
In a 2022 interview, the poet Olesya Nikolaeva (wife of Russian Orthodox Church priest Vladimir Vigilyansky) characterized the war in Ukraine as “a clash of civilizations: Christian, on the one hand, and one that has renounced Christ and sunk into paganism, if not Satanism, on the other.” The Satanists, one must understand, are Western civilization.
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 turned out to be neither swift nor victorious, with Russian troops taking months to capture every tiny village — only to lose it after a few more weeks of intense fighting. For now, Mala Tokmachka remains as inaccessible for Russian patriots as the straits for the 19th-century empire. Yet throughout 2022, inertia inspired poets to keep holding onto their pre-war mood of swaggering overconfidence.
That year, Igor Karaulov wrote a humorous poem that begins with the line: “Let us split Poland right in half, like the sweet iceberg of a Kyiv cake...” — as if the division of the “Kyiv” cake were still a foregone conclusion, a prelude to Russia’s conquest of its old lands further west.
The poet Maria Vatutina, whose poems are now available both on the YouTube channel of Russia’s National Guard and on the TV channel Russky Mir, borrows images of “liberator warriors” from Soviet propaganda:
The old men wept upon his chest,
The roadside villages shone bright,
They’re planting flowers in Mariupol,
And bringing textbooks to the schools.
Hopes for a swift redrawing of the borders across the post-Soviet space are reflected in Alexander Pelevin’s “In the City of Limonov” (2022), in which the author renames the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, the hometown of Russian writer Eduard Limonov (1943-2020):
In the city of Limonov 
Padded jackets fill the streets
Public holidays and street names 
Will be changing before long.  
As we’re rising in our millions, 
Like we did when we were young, 
In the city of Limonov, 
Kharkiv Region — that’s the one.  
We are not bad people — our history is the problem
By 2026 the full-scale invasion of Ukraine had long since evolved into positional, trench warfare — striking in the irrational number of casualties taken for every captured kilometer. Poetry has to somehow justify such a high price, but after 2023, the names of captured settlements appear less often in propagandist art while the poet’s gaze turns to the metaphysical depths of the war. This change of optics helps to soothe the anxious reader — and the poet’s own conscience.
As could be expected, pro-war poetry usually chooses the “warrior of light” as its lyrical hero. But in moments of doubt, a characteristic ethical reversal kicks in, familiar to us from the Kremlin propaganda after 2014. Generally, “we” are the best, kindest, and most honest. But in the absence of extolling arguments — as in the case of Russian athletes caught doping — the “ethical reversal” kicks in, with propaganda whispering that “everybody does it; we are not the bad guys — everyone else is no better.”
The poet Alexander Pelevin employs this device when reflecting on the future:
There will be no “good Russian” passports for you,
Who’s good and who’s bad — who can tell from a trench?
We live in grim times, and since we are the bad guys,
Well, glory to Russia — what more can I say?
This marks an important turn: the “patriotic” poet realizes that a “good war” is no longer possible, and advises his readers to get used to being bad. He grasps at big ideas to justify this new position: the image of an ominous “History” appears in Pelevin’s poetry, an entity that simply exists regardless of people’s will. And this “History” of his is by definition a malevolent, cruel actor, meaning outsiders are not entitled to hold our actions against us:
History smells of death, history smells of sh*t,
History is burned-out vehicles, rust-covered metal scrap,
History is when they say: wherever you see him, kill him.
History is what happens when some people kill other people.
Propaganda in 2023-2024 also turned to a “historical” argument as justification, portraying the war against Ukraine as inevitable — the legacy of the Soviet Union’s collapse postponed by 30 years, something that “had to happen” and “could not have been avoided” (a thought Dmitry Medvedev expressed in one of his articles in the spring of 2023).
Seeking resonance with these ever-changing “root causes” of the war, propagandist poets mimic the state’s arguments: “we did not start it,” “we were set against each other,” and besides, Ukraine is “torn by civil war.”
Propagandist poets mimic the state’s arguments in their poems: “we did not start it,” “we were set against each other,” and besides, Ukraine is “torn by civil war”
The poet Sveta Litvak works in the genre of playful performance — a deliberate device reminiscent of “children’s poems” in the spirit of Agniya Barto. A brisk stepped-line verse seems intended to help readers memorize the theses of propaganda by heart:
You know, Sergeant, we’ll have company tonight.
The hostile silence shrouds the town before the fight.
As long as brother murders brother,
After one battle comes another,
Placing an end to war beyond our sight.
The wind from the Atlantic brings us hostile hordes,
One nation set against the other by their lords.
(2024)
In trying to explain the length of the war, nationalist poetry first relies, in the spirit of state patriotism, on the thesis that this war is not new but rather a “continuation of the Great Patriotic War,” which supposedly never ended:
Our great-grandfather drove out the plague,
was captured and escaped,
and held his head high in Berlin, and to us
bequeathed his fate — to beat the enemy
Imagine that, one with its center in Kyiv.
(A poem by a mobilized man named Nikita that came out in 2023 in the collection “Resurrected in the Third World War,” distributed free of charge through the public services portal Gosuslugi)
There is also another argument, borrowed from the Soviet playbook of the Cold War era, that has come to the pro-war poet’s aid. This is “not just any war” but the Third World War, the worst fear of all Soviet children. The anthology of pro-war poetry that came out in early 2023, edited by pro-Kremlin author Zakhar Prilepin, is called exactly that — “Resurrected in the Third World War.” (It sold roughly 10,000 copies).
Following Putin, who has repeated many times that the “special military operation” will last as long as it takes to achieve the mysterious “goals” known only to him, the poet Anna Dolgareva — nicknamed the “Valkyrie of the special military operation” — gives this message a simple and clear form:
Death is inevitable (here, a shot booms like a chord).
“How much longer?” As long as your sense of duty can last.
For in Russia one must live long
And die fast.
Russian pro-war poetry stands out from among other genres of propaganda by sometimes letting slip the truth — even if inadvertently. In the classic definition of a totalitarian state, a citizen has only one duty: to die for their fatherland quickly, without thinking and without asking questions.
Igor Karaulov, a representative of an older generation, is in no hurry to give straightforward explanations. In a 2023 interview he frankly admits that he had not expected the war to drag on. And to the question “Who are we fighting?” he gives what seems to him a paradoxical and wise answer: “Ourselves.”
Russian pro-war poetry stands out from among other propaganda genres by sometimes letting slip the truth — if inadvertently
The main prewar mythologem held that, as a result of a hypothetical war, Russian society was supposed to “be cleansed.” But since society has yet to cleanse itself fully or sufficiently, the war cannot end in victory. This presents an example of outstanding semantic acrobatics on the part of poet Karaulov, who demonstrates just how elastic a patriot’s logic can be: cause and effect, the horse and the cart, easily switch places if need be — whenever and however is convenient for the author.
To justify the number of casualties and the length of the invasion, pro-war poets have to keep expanding its purpose. Karaulov himself writes:
A stock of warmth, a stock of hardtack,
My dear old lumbering bear,
Our motherland’s rockets streak overhead,
A Mandelstam lying facedown by the bed.
In a bout of remarkable cynicism, the author rhymes Osip Mandelstam — who was tortured and killed by the Stalinist regime and was far removed from any motives of military conquest — with Putin’s missiles.
Remarkably, this device closely follows the state’s own approach. In 2017, educational posters printed to mark the occasion of Moscow’s 870th anniversary appeared on the capital’s streets and in the subway, illustrating the city’s history with the fates of its outstanding residents. The city administration did not hesitate to claim for itself the achievements of Great Terror victims like the geneticist Nikolai Vavilov or the poet Osip Mandelstam.
Not all metaphorical allies have to be native-born. The poet Olesya Nikolaeva, claims for herself a composer from a country that modern-day Russia treats as unfriendly:
Who stands with us? Our kin, our blood,
The running river, rustling forests, love,
The golden skies, the secret breath of spring,
And all of Mozart, and prophetic dreams.
And yet, in the fifth year of war, poets and composers alone will not do: higher powers have to be called in. As a result, in Anna Dolgareva’s poems, God, angels, and camouflage-clad saints often descend into dugouts, don body armor, smoke with soldiers, and share the hardships of war. This running plot can be seen in other pro-war poets as well.
God is with us; so is the sun; and so is the rain
that loaded its sniper rifle.
(Anna Revyakina, the poem “The Miner’s Daughter”).
In Sofia Yudina’s poem “To the Hospital,” God comes in a greatcoat (in this image one recognizes, however, rather an earthly god — Joseph Stalin):
It is as though God comes home every night,
Takes off his shabby army greatcoat, hangs it
On a hook, then stomps to shake the snow off his boots,
Turns on the light, and looks — and through the blizzard
Starlight begins to glimmer over weary earth.
Alongside furious appeals to the forces of light, propagandist poetry also takes pride in a secret ability to “make hell” on earth. Speaking on behalf of the light, poets do not miss the chance to wink at the lower tier. Dolgareva again:
The commander said it as a simple fact:
“We raised hell
On sectors facing not battalions —
But whole brigades.”
They were foretold
To burn up, not hold out for long.
They offered a preview —
Showed what hell is like.
Chumminess with hell is a distinct feature of Russian pro-war poetry — a device that could be interpreted as a perverse way of “making peace with the war.” Hell, blood, coffins, and the cross that must be borne are frequent images in the work Dolgareva and others, where blood, guts, and mud are invoked not to appall the reader but as a kind of paean to this hell on earth:
And yet,
Even if my tongue should die,
I will pronounce this all the same
Into this
Horror mixed with the remains of bodies,
Into this sunset pink
And air blue,
To my last breath:
“Russia,
Glory be with you.”
As literary scholar Oleg Lekmanov noted in 2024: “The candy-sweet prettiness with the epithet and the noun swapped places (‘sunset pink,’ ‘air blue’) is no accident next to ‘the remains of bodies’ — these images are meant to be perceived in one row. It looks as if today’s [pro-war] poets have gotten hooked on the cruelty and blood of war like heavy narcotics.”
Finally, one more way to justify war is a paradoxical and deliberate admiration for it, a kind of infernal bravado. The collection by the poet Dmitry Artis is titled “He Walks Through the War,” cynically paraphrasing Gennady Shpalikov’s anthem of the Sixties generation. Philologist Mikhail Edelstein calls Artis “one of the bloodthirstiest poets in this crowd.” His deliberate cruelty contains a disinterested rapture before death:
War is a piece of happiness,
a blood-soaked chunk,
A gem of freedom
without a slavish cut…
War is the very best mother
That we could have,
The taste of porridge
She gave us when we were young.
Over the past five years, the meaning of the war in Russian “patriotic” poetry has performed an astonishing somersault from the promise of a swift national victory in 2022 to a wish in 2026 for everyone involved to have “a good death.”
At his infamous meeting with the mothers of killed mobilized soldiers in 2022, Vladimir Putin quoted lines by the celebrated Soviet poet and songwriter Vladimir Vysotsky: “To go this way is better than from vodka and from colds.” The Kremlin’s attempt to enlist even Vysotsky as an ally in its deadly escapade is no more cynical than everything else. After all, the very idea of a “sacrificial, meaningful death” is a trademark device of Soviet propaganda. Unsurprisingly, this motif also appears in the poems of Igor Karaulov:
Others flee to the front to escape their death.
Where steel goddesses rage, where the guns never tire.
Where the grain that must perish will never expire.
The image of fallen soldiers “sprouting” after death in the form of grass is another popular trope — in the work of Maria Vatutina, in particular:
Like stalks, we shoot up, bud by bud,
We sprout, dead, through tight-packed soil,
We lift our heads, beginning to be heard.
Soon we will reign as kings, as wordsmiths of the world.
Literary scholar Mikhail Edelstein unambiguously interprets this passage as presenting an image of the resurrected dead who will come to “reign as kings,” and more than that, this infernal side of pro-war poetry also marks the evident exhaustion of rational arguments for the war among poets and officials alike. This is called magical thinking: when reality does not match the basic myth, one has to pile up ever more new myths.
Instilling the idea that one must get used to an endless, pointless war is the only purpose poetic propaganda can serve today. The same goes, indeed, for Kremlin propaganda as a whole.

articles.title: Czech Mars 4×4 gets twin machine guns for drone defense
articles.body:
- Czech 25th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment troops test-fired a Gladius Twin twin-machine-gun station on an SVOS Mars 4x4 against small drones at Boletice.
- The trials checked a Czech Ministry of Defence study; no order for the configuration has been announced.
Czech air defense troops have test-fired a remotely operated twin machine gun mounted on SVOS’s Mars 4×4 armored vehicle against small drones, as Czech industry offers the vehicle as a cheaper counter-drone option alongside the missile-armed version the Army of the Czech Republic has already ordered.
Soldiers from the 25th Anti-Aircraft Missile Regiment in Strakonice ran the trials at the Boletice military training area in southern Bohemia, using small, low-cost drones as targets. They first checked how well the electro-optical sensors on the Gladius Twin weapon station could detect and track the drones, and then fired live rounds at them. SVOS, which builds the Mars 4×4 in Přelouč, developed the configuration with EVPÚ Defence, the maker of the Gladius Twin, which carries two 7.62 mm machine guns and is mounted on the Mars 4×4 S-330 Hard Top variant. The companies did not say when the trials took place, how many drones were flown, at what ranges they were engaged or how many were hit.
The firing tests were meant to check in practice the conclusions of a Czech Ministry of Defence study on fitting the Gladius Twin to the Mars 4×4, which the state-owned Military Technical Institute and its aviation branch prepared for the army. According to the announcement, the trials showed that the weapon station worked effectively within the range of its ammunition and sensors, that it is suitable for integration on the Mars 4×4 for close-in air defense as part of force protection, and that cooperation with domestic industry pays off for the army.
The machine gun version is the second air defense configuration SVOS has shown on the Mars 4×4, following the vehicle armed with Saab’s RBS 70 NG laser-guided missiles. In July 2025, the Czech Ministry of Defence signed a contract worth about SEK 1.86 billion (about $195 million) with Saab for 24 Mars 4×4 vehicles carrying RBS 70 NG launchers, with SVOS as a subcontractor, plus eight tripod-mounted launchers and 80 missiles. Those vehicles are due to reach three batteries of the same 25th regiment between 2028 and 2030, replacing a mix of older RBS 70 and RBS 70 NG launchers that the unit currently operates in dismounted form, with crews exposed while firing.
Machine guns guided by a stabilized electro-optical sight give a much cheaper way to deal with small drones at short range than missiles, which can cost far more than the drones they shoot down. A weapon station like the Gladius Twin can also cover the final few hundred meters around a unit or base, where small reconnaissance and attack drones are most dangerous to troops on the ground.
SVOS says the Mars 4×4 already forms the basis of the Czech mobile short-range air defense system and has the technical features needed to carry other weapon systems.

articles.title: FSB detains Russian woman over Ukraine-backed plot to attack military airfield
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 13. /TASS/. Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has detained a Russian woman suspected of preparing a drone attack on a military airfield on orders from the Security Service of Ukraine, the FSB said in a statement.
"The Federal Security Service in the Voronezh Region has foiled a large-scale act of sabotage and terrorism orchestrated by the Security Service of Ukraine, which planned to attack the Russian Defense Ministry’s Baltimor military airfield with short-range drones," the statement reads.
Law enforcement operations made it possible to expose and disrupt the illegal activities of a Russian woman who had been recruited by a Ukrainian intelligence officer during a trip to Ukraine in 2022. "Acting on instructions from her handler, she traveled to Voronezh and rented a garage, where she planned to assemble and launch drones meant to be used to destroy infrastructure and aircraft, as well as kill military airfield staff," the FSB said. The drones were supposed to be operated remotely by personnel based in Ukraine.
According to the FSB, the woman retrieved nine drones equipped with explosive devices, along with drone control equipment, from previously established caches and took them to the garage. Each drone carried 500 grams of foreign-made explosives.
"FSB officers responded immediately after receiving intel, promptly detaining the accomplice of Ukrainian intelligence agencies and preventing the act of sabotage before it was carried out, thus containing the potential consequences of the Kiev regime’s actions against the military facility," the agency stressed.
The suspect has been taken into custody. "Efforts are ongoing to establish all circumstances of the crime and identify all those involved," the FSB added.

articles.title: Russian Radio Gives Away Infiltration Route—Ukraine’s Special Forces Set a Trap
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russian Radio Gives Away Infiltration Route—Ukraine’s Special Forces Set a Trap
Ukrainian Special Operations Forces (SSO) have disrupted a Russian infiltration route in the Donetsk direction, killing three Russian soldiers and capturing another during an ambush carried out by operators of the 3rd Special Operations Brigade’s Sword Group.
The operation was announced by Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces on Facebook on October 12, where the military also released footage of the raid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the SSO, Ukrainian operators initially raided a shelter used by Russian troops as a temporary resting and assembly point. During the operation, they seized a radio that revealed several additional Russian groups were expected to move along the same route.
Using the intercepted information, Ukrainian special forces remained at the position and prepared an ambush for the approaching Russian troops. The subsequent engagement resulted in three Russian soldiers being killed and one taken prisoner.
“The prisoner was carrying a radio and a mobile phone containing checkpoints and alternative routes of advance in the area. He also provided the call signs of Russian commanders and other valuable intelligence,” the statement read.
During questioning, the prisoner reportedly described Russian military tactics involving repeated infantry assaults, often referred to as “meat assaults,” as well as discriminatory treatment of ethnic minorities within the Russian army.
According to the SSO, the prisoner also alleged that Russian troops were prohibited from assisting wounded personnel and that soldiers who refused orders could be killed by their own forces.
Ukrainian special operations personnel said they had observed similar practices among Russian troops operating in the area.
The commander of the 3rd Special Operations Regiment further described how Russian forces allegedly deploy personnel from ethnic minority groups in initial assault waves before sending additional units to consolidate captured positions.
“Most often, we encounter Yakuts, Buryats, Tajiks, and Uzbeks here. They are sent forward as cannon fodder, and then their other units, move in and secure strategic positions,” the commander explained.
Ukrainian military intelligence operatives eliminated two Russian special forces groups during a counter-sabotage operation in the Zaporizhzhia direction, capturing one Russian soldier after tracking the units’ movements and preparing an ambush.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) reported on October 11 that the operation was conducted by its Timur Special Unit against troops from Russia’s 10th Separate Guards Special Purpose Brigade, which operates under Russian military intelligence.

articles.title: Europe must switch to ‘war-mode’ defence production, Polish defence minister says
articles.body:
Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that Europe must accelerate the production of ammunition and weapons to match Russia’s pace, warning that failure to do so would negatively impact Europe.
Poland’s Minister of National Defence and Deputy Prime Minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, said Europe must adopt a “war-mode” mentality in its defence sector or risk harming Europeans in the future.
“I am actually an advocate for the war-mode when it comes to the production in defence sector,” he said at a press conference on the sidelines of the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.
“This is what the Russian Federation does at the moment. We cannot overlook this fact.”
Russia shifted towards wartime defence production before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and is projected to spend 7.5% of its gross domestic product on its armed forces in 2026.
In 2025, Russia produced roughly seven million artillery, mortar, tank and rocket rounds, according to a recent Estonian intelligence report. Russian forces currently use roughly 10,000 to 15,000 rounds per day in their continued aggression against Ukraine.
In contrast, Europe’s defence industry has been shaped by decades of underinvestment and fragmentation.
Russia is outpacing the EU in ammunition production, with the 27 member states and Norway expected to produce just two million 150mm ammunition shells this year, according to a leaked report on Europe’s defence readiness.
Rearmament efforts by European countries and NATO members have driven the strongest annual increase in defence spending since the Cold War. Despite this, EU member states’ total defence spending in 2025 was estimated at €418 billion, or 2.2% of EU's total GDP, the report states.
Kosiniak-Kamysz said the “time has come” for Europe to prepare to defend itself by multiplying its defence production.
Failure to do so would be a “costly” mistake for Europeans, he warned, adding: “It's one of the disadvantages, but also it will impact (and) affect us negatively in future generations.”
Poland is among the biggest spenders of its GDP on defence capabilities, spending 4.7% on core defence capabilities, according to the US envoy to NATO, Matthew Whitaker.

articles.title: Iran eyes African markets through technology cooperation with Senegal
articles.body:
Iran eyes African markets through technology cooperation with Senegal
TEHRAN – Iranian officials have explored ways to strengthen scientific and technological cooperation with Senegal, positioning the West African country as a gateway for Iranian knowledge-based companies seeking to expand into African markets.
Hossein Roozbeh, head of the Organization for the Development of International Cooperation in Science and Technology, met with Hamid Moradkhani, Iran’s ambassador to Senegal, on Saturday to discuss avenues for expanding bilateral cooperation, IRNA reported.
The talks focused on boosting exports of knowledge-based products, transferring technical expertise for the production of agricultural drones, and finalizing a comprehensive memorandum of understanding (MoU) on technological cooperation between the two countries.
The officials also discussed ways to benefit from artificial intelligence (AI) capacities and technological infrastructures to develop bilateral economic relations.
Describing Senegal as a gateway for Iranian technology to the African continent, Roozbeh put forward several proposals to expand bilateral cooperation.
He noted that more than 11,000 knowledge-based companies operate in Iran, producing goods that meet international standards and compete with their global counterparts in both quality and price.
He also announced Iran’s readiness for joint manufacturing of products in agricultural, medical, petrochemical, and energy sectors.
His other suggestion focused on establishing and developing science and technology parks and Iranian innovation centers in Senegal.
Holding technological exhibitions, providing specialized content for media in Senegal, granting scholarships to Senegalese students, and hosting Senegalese technical delegations in the Iranian House of Innovation and Technology (iHiT) were among other points suggested by the official.
For his part, Moradkhani highlighted technology transfer and specialized training as the key pillars of the two countries’ collaborations, and called for the Vice Presidency for Science and Technology to play an active role in Iran-Africa joint commissions.
He also underscored the importance of establishing a network of experts and strengthening exchanges in the oil and energy sectors.
The official added that a draft memorandum of understanding (MoU) had been finalized and was expected to be signed during a visit to Tehran by senior Senegalese officials in January 2027.
Tehran hosts meeting of African envoys to boost science, health cooperation
On December 7, 2025, Iranian officials and the ambassadors of 19 African countries to Tehran discussed ways to enhance cooperation in the fields of science, education, research, and health.
Addressing the meeting, held in Tehran, Nader Tavakoli, the Chancellor of Iran University of Medical Sciences, said despite coercive sanctions, the country has managed to make great strides in the health sector, from education and treatment to technology and production of medicines, relying on committed and creative human resources, IRNA reported.
“Now, we are ready to share these achievements with Africans through establishing a strategic health alliance between Iran and African countries,” Tavakoli highlighted.
Elaborating on the core areas of the strategic alliance, he said that researchers will focus on addressing real-time illnesses, such as tropical and endemic diseases, drug shortages, and health service delivery in rural areas.
Admitting African students and developing joint educational courses, with dual accreditation, as well as dispatching professors for training of trainers, will be another part of the alliance.
Other main components of the strategic alliance will include sharing technical knowledge in fields such as manufacturing vaccines, biosimilar drugs, and medical equipment by establishing a collaborative production line in African countries, Tavakoli added.
The expansion of scientific interactions between Iranian and African scientists was the last point mentioned by the official. The strategic alliance will lay the basis for boosting scientific collaborations between over 60 universities and hundreds of top research centers across the country, he further noted.
On December 8, the ministries of health and foreign affairs, in a virtual meeting with Iranian ambassadors and attachés in Africa, discussed the potential for promoting cooperation with African countries in the health sector.
During the meeting, Alireza Biglari, the deputy health minister for international affairs, highlighted the country’s capabilities in areas related to health. Referring to the existing capacity as a valuable opportunity for the expansion of health diplomacy and the favorable condition for cooperation with African countries, the official announced the readiness of the health ministry to implement decisions and operational plans, IRNA reported.
For his part, Akbar Khosravi Nejad, Assistant to Iran’s Foreign Minister and Director General for Africa, underlined the importance of Africa in Iran’s foreign policy, and said that the country’s health system is one of the main sectors for enhancing collaborations with these countries.
Tavakoli, for his part, presented an account of the current activities and programs of the university in Africa, as well as future plans to meet African ambassadors in Tehran.

articles.title: Spox Ihnat: Russia deploys about 200 jet-powered drones per day
articles.body:
Spox Ihnat: Russia deploys about 200 jet-powered drones per day
According to Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, made this statement during a television broadcast.
“Right now, it’s about 100 during the day and 100 at night—and that’s just counting jet-powered UAVs. They also combine them with other drones,” Ihnat said.
According to him, the Ukrainian military is gradually improving its effectiveness in intercepting jet-powered drones thanks to the experience gained, but Ukraine needs additional missiles and ammunition for ground-based air defense systems and aviation.
He noted that even a small number of drones that reach their targets can cause significant damage to Ukrainian facilities.
As previously reported, Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, stated that Russia is stepping up its use of jet-powered drones to attack Ukraine: while it used about 350 such UAVs in June, it used about 3,500 in September.
